FACTUAL INFORMATION
Narrative
JCK’s skipper, Andrew Westaway, met with the skipper of Bold Venture at around 0645 on the morning
of 28 January. They considered various weather forecasts before sailing from Torquay, Devon, including
a general forecast from the television, the shipping forecast from the Met Office and a forecast from the
internet website “Magicseaweed”. Although the weather forecasts predicted strong offshore winds during
the late afternoon, it was the skippers’ perception that the weather would follow the same pattern as the
previous 2 days, with the strongest winds occurring during the night, by which time they were expecting
to be back in Torquay.
Following discussions centred on the day ahead, the skippers prepared their boats for sea. JCK and
Bold Venture sailed from Torquay at 0745.
JCK and Bold Venture arrived at Babbacombe Bay (Figure 2) at about 0815, where the skippers
commenced hauling their nets which had been set in the area the previous day. Fishing was good and,
after hauling, the two boats secured to a mooring buoy off Babbacombe pier (Figure 3) to fleet1 their
nets, which then took several hours.
JCK’s herring net was seen to have fished better than that of Bold Venture and also it was a significantly
easier net from which to remove the herring. The skippers agreed that shooting only JCK’s net that night
would probably yield sufficient catch for both boats the following morning, and that Bold Venture would
therefore return to port with her net on board.
Around mid-afternoon the wind increased notably from the SW, evidenced by the clouds scudding across
the sky above the cliff tops. The increased wind also delivered persistent rain and drizzle.
At about 1710 Bold Venture’s skipper stopped fleeting his herring net and headed towards Hope’s Nose
(Figure 2) to check the conditions beyond the shelter of the land, while Andrew shot his herring net.
Bold Venture’s skipper returned, and explained to Andrew that he did not like the look of the conditions.
Andrew considered this, but thought that both vessels should proceed to Hope’s Nose to review the sea
conditions.
Before setting off, the boats were bailed out and their catch and gear stowed for a homeward passage.
Andrew stacked five boxes of catch on each side of JCK and stowed a further five baskets of catch
towards the bow. Bold Venture’s catch and net (still containing herring) were stowed in boxes forward
and aft of the thwart, between the longitudinal buoyancy chambers. Neither skipper donned the
inflatable lifejackets carried on board.
In late twilight the boats rounded Hope’s Nose with JCK in the lead and Bold Venture following. Between
Lead Stone and Thatcher Rock the boats encountered strong south-westerly winds and heavy seas,
resulting in both shipping significant amounts of water. Nevertheless, they continued between Thatcher
Rock and the land, gaining a brief lee from Thatcher Rock (Figures 4a and 4b).
JCK stopped a few hundred metres beyond Thatcher Rock. As Bold Venture passed close by, Andrew
was seen rearranging boxes of catch and bailing. A short distance beyond JCK, the skipper of Bold
Venture stopped and waited for JCK, also taking the opportunity to bail out at this time. JCK was seen
making way again with Andrew seated at the stern by the outboard engine’s tiller. Bold Venture’s skipper
engaged his engine and resumed passage, but now in the lead, towards Torquay. Every now and then
he looked astern and saw the lights of JCK following.

After clearing East Shag (Figures 4a and 4b) conditions worsened, with wind gusts exceeding 50 knots
at times. Bold Venture’s skipper was forced to tack his vessel in a zig-zag fashion as waves crashed
down on the boat, often blinding him with sea spray. During this time Bold Venture’s skipper did not dare
look behind; terrified to take his eyes from the oncoming seas he made a conscious decision to not stop
and bail out, despite his boat shipping large quantities of water.
Bold Venture eventually gained the safety of Torquay harbour at around 1810.
The search
Immediately Bold Venture was alongside the skipper attempted to call Andrew’s mobile telephone, with
no success. A few minutes later he was met on the pier by Andrew’s father. Together they looked for
JCK, but the vessel was not visible either from the pier or from the shoreline towards Thatcher Rock.
At 1853 the coastguard was notified, and a comprehensive search was immediately initiated involving
numerous SAR2 assets, a naval frigate and other vessels.
Andrew’s body was found at 2351, over 3 miles to the north of Hope’s Nose. The cause of death was
drowning.
JCK was not found, although some flotsam was recovered.
Environment
The Met Office forecast for the 24-hour period commencing at 0600 on 28 January 2013 predicted
“very windy weather to all areas…” and, specifically between Lands End and Lyme Bay, “west backing
southwest 5 to 7, increasing 7 to severe gale 9”. The Magicseaweed internet site predicted generally
south-westerly winds of 30 to 34mph with gusts reaching 56mph in the period from 1500 to 1800 (Figure
5).

position) for the afternoon of 28 January were:

Vessel details
JCK
JCK was an Orkney Fastliner 19 design, built around 1987 and first registered as a fishing vessel in
2008. JCK was acquired by Andrew Westaway in April 2009.
It is not known who fitted out the original boat, although the glass reinforced plastic (GRP) hull was most
likely moulded by Orkney Boats Ltd as one of its commercial Fastliner 19 models. Orkney Boats Ltd also
built similar Fastliner 19 models for the leisure sector that were lighter than, and not as strong as, the
commercial models. In order to give more internal space, the commercial model Fastliner 19 (Figure 6)
was not equipped with the side chambers and central thwart found on the standard model (Figure 7).
JCK had no manufacturer’s or recreational craft directive (RCD) plate; at the time the vessel was built,
neither was required.
On 20 May 2009 JCK suffered flooding due to the self-draining “elephant trunks” being left deployed
while alongside. When the bow line was cast off to enable a recovery vessel alongside, JCK sank by
the bow, leaving only its stern supported by the mooring line. Following this incident the water damaged
60hp outboard engine was replaced with a more powerful and heavier 70hp model, plus an additional
starting battery.
JCK carried the required equipment for a vessel of its size as listed in the Fishing Vessels Code of
Practice for the Safety of Small Fishing Vessels (MSN3 1813). Among other things, this included
lifejackets, pyrotechnics, lights and VHF4 radio. However, JCK’s radio had been left ashore as it was
faulty, and communications were carried out by mobile telephone instead. On 28 January Andrew’s
mobile telephone went off the air at 1650, about 25 minutes before the vessel left Babbacombe Bay.
It is calculated that the payload (engine, batteries, fuel, catch etc.) carried on board JCK on 28 January
weighed about 735kg.
3 MSN: Merchant Shipping Notice
4 VHF: Very High Frequency
8
Image courtesy of Orkney Boats Ltd
Buoyancy chamber
Figure 6: Orkney Boats Ltd, Commercial Model Fastliner 19.
Note: no central thwart or side chambers
Fleeting bar
Side chamber
Thwart
Figure 7: Bold Venture
9
Bold Venture
Bold Venture was an Orkney Boats Ltd standard model Fastliner 19. Due to its lighter construction, Bold
Venture sat higher in the water than JCK and could obtain more speed with its less powerful and lighter
25hp outboard engine.
Bold Venture had a manufacturer’s plate (Figure 8), which showed its maximum carrying capacity of
490kg and maximum recommended engine capacity of 40hp.
Like JCK, Bold Venture carried most of the required equipment for a vessel of its size, but no radio as it
was no longer operational.
It is calculated that Bold Venture’s payload on 28 January was about 640kg, of which 342kg was fish
catch.
Figure 8: Bold Venture’s manufacturer’s plate
Fishing operation
When acquired by Andrew, JCK was rigged for rod and line fishing. Andrew continued this mode of
fishing but, in addition, modified the vessel for gill net fishing (netting). Modifications included the addition
of a net hauler and side roller to assist with net retrieval and a head-high gantry (known as a fleeting bar)
to facilitate clearing and preparation of the nets.
Andrew’s preferred operation was line fishing for bass on offshore wrecks; a low-volume, high-value
species of fish. During winter months, when it was not possible to reach distant wrecks, Andrew chose to
net for high-volume, low-value herring and mackerel closer to the shore. Netting required the carriage of
bulky nets and relatively heavy anchors and ropes. When equipped for netting, JCK had a constant trim
by the head.
10
The nets used by JCK were approximately 160m x 3m of fine netting, which hung in curtain-like
suspension between the seabed and the surface, with an anchor at each end. Nets were generally shot
before darkness and hauled at daylight the following day.
The nets were recovered from the sea with the assistance of a mechanical rotating hauler. Once on
board, the nets were re-hauled (fleeted) over the fleeting bar; during the fleeting process fish were
removed either by shaking them from the nets or, more often, taken out by hand to preserve their quality.
Fish were stored on board in 20kg boxes and 32kg baskets. On 28 January JCK had 10 boxes and 5
baskets of catch, approximating to a total weight of catch of 360kg.
Generally, JCK fished from Torquay, from where the catch was transported by road to Brixham fish
market.
Key persons
Andrew Westaway (deceased)
Andrew was aged 46 and had been a career fisherman for over 20 years. Although he mostly operated
JCK single handedly, he had previously fished the boat in partnership with his father. Since his father’s
retirement, Andrew often fished in the company of Bold Venture; at times the two skippers would go to
sea in one boat to reduce costs when fishing distant wrecks.
Andrew held mandatory training certificates in: Basic Sea Survival, Basic First Aid, Basic Fire fighting,
Safety Awareness and Risk Assessment. He also held a Sea Fish Industry Authority (Seafish) non-
mandatory under 16.5m Skipper’s Certificate having achieving the required standards in: Bridge
Watchkeeping, Engine Room Watchkeeping, Intermediate Stability Awareness and GMDSS5 short-range
radio certificate.
Andrew did not wear a lifejacket when fishing, although at times he did wear a thermal flotation suit for
warmth; he was not wearing his thermal flotation suit on 28 January.
Bold Venture’s skipper
The skipper of Bold Venture was 48 years old and had fished sporadically for about 7 years in total.
In 2010 he became skipper of Bold Venture. Soon after this he became friendly with Andrew, and
commonly deferred to his greater local knowledge and fishing experience.
Bold Venture’s skipper held Seafish equivalent mandatory training certification in Basic Sea Survival,
Basic First Aid, and Basic Fire fighting; he had not attended Safety Awareness and Risk Assessment
training.
Bold Venture’s skipper did not wear a PFD6 as he considered them to be hazardous (due to potential
snagging) when working fishing gear.
5 GMDSS: Global Maritime Distress and Safety System.
6 PFD: Personal Flotation Device: the generic title for all dedicated equipment which provides some degree of support for its
wearer in the water. This can include: lifejackets, buoyancy aids/vests, immersion suits and flotation suits. It should be noted
that, unlike lifejackets, not all PFDs maintain an unconscious wearer’s face clear of the water.
11
ANALYSIS
It is most probable that JCK foundered at around 1750 between Thatcher Rock and Torquay harbour. At
this time winds were gusting around 52 knots in the area, causing a rough sea state with waves probably
in excess of 4m. JCK was heavily laden with her day’s catch and equipment, which would have impaired
her sea-keeping abilities in such severe conditions.
Decision to fish
The skippers of JCK and Bold Venture shot their nets in Babbacombe Bay on 27 January in the
expectation of strong south-westerly winds. Once shot, however, commercial pressure required that the
nets be hauled the following day, otherwise their perishable catch would spoil and be worthless.
Fishing in Babbacombe Bay in south-westerly winds was a sound commercial decision – the shelter
afforded by the high cliffs enabled the boats to fish in comfort and safety. Additionally, market prices are
frequently higher when fishing vessels are storm-bound by weather with a resultant limited supply of fish.
While the skippers gave due consideration to their ability to fish, they did not make contingency plans
should the weather conditions make their return to Torquay too dangerous. These contingencies could
have included:
• Hauling their nets and immediately returning to Torquay to fleet them (but thereby losing their
next day’s catch and wages).
• Hauling their nets and landing their catch at Babbacombe pier for road transport to Brixham,
then mooring to the pier or one of the numerous mooring buoys in the bay overnight. This
would also have ensured their next day’s fishing had continuing south-westerly wind or sea
state prevented a passage from Torquay on 29 January.
Had the skippers discussed these options prior to sailing, they would have been more likely to adopt a
safer plan, after assessing the conditions from Hope’s Nose.
Environment
The weather forecasts from Magicseaweed and the Met Office predicted the conditions with
considerable accuracy. Before sailing on the morning of 28 January, the skippers of JCK and Bold
Venture evaluated these and other forecasts but perceived that they would be back in harbour before the
forecast strong winds arrived.
The weather records from nearby Berry Head and Tor Bay NCI show the wind increased throughout the
afternoon of 28 January and peaked around the time JCK and Bold Venture were between Thatcher
Rock and Torquay. The Tor Bay NCI recorded actual sea states as “rough” (2.5m to 4.0m) up until they
closed late that afternoon. The winds increased to 52 knots between then and 1800, and it is most likely
the waves were over 4.0m high around the time JCK was lost.
The wind direction was forecast to be offshore in Tor Bay, which gave the skippers some peace of mind
before they sailed. However, during south-westerly winds there is a fetch of 3.5 nautical miles between
the Goodrington shore (Figures 4a and 4b) and Thatcher Rock, causing high waves to develop towards
the Thatcher Rock area. Given Andrew’s experience and local knowledge it is doubtful that he was not
aware of this fetch and the associated wave heights with south-westerly winds in the area.
Sunset was at 1647 on 28 January. The heavily overcast sky hastened darkness, and before the boats
reached Thatcher Rock, night had fallen. A small open boat’s sea passage in such conditions would
have been extremely hazardous in daylight, but would have been further exacerbated by darkness.
12
Boats and loading
JCK was a heavily constructed GRP Fastliner 19; Bold Venture was a lighter standard model. Both
boats were constructed with inherent buoyancy designed to support a flooded boat and payload of its
recommended carrying capacity. In Bold Venture’s case this would have been 490kg, as indicated
by her manufacturer’s plate (Figure 8). Due to her age, JCK had no such plate, but later Fastliner 19
commercial models built by Orkney Boats Ltd had a similar recommended carrying capacity to that of
Bold Venture.
On 20 May 2009 JCK flooded in Torquay harbour, and only the mooring lines prevented the vessel from
sinking. This would suggest that JCK’s inherent buoyancy was impaired, possibly as a result of GRP
bonding damage in the 26 year old craft. JCK was not found after Andrew’s death, probably as a result
of sinking in the severe sea conditions at the time. Had the inherent buoyancy been intact the boat
should have been washed ashore at some point.
On 28 January both boats were heavily laden with catch and gear on their return passage. It is
considered that Bold Venture was carrying about 640kg while JCK was carrying about 735kg – between
30% and 50% more weight than Orkney Boats Ltd recommended for Fastliner 19s. Although both boats
had over 300kg of catch on board, inspection of catch records showed they had regularly carried greater
loads in good weather conditions. The difference in payload between the two boats on 28 January is
attributed mainly to JCK’s heavier engine, additional battery and greater catch. These loads, in such
conditions, would certainly have dampened the boats’ abilities to rise to oncoming seas and would have
reduced their overall sea-keeping abilities.
JCK’s catch was stowed in boxes stacked five high port and starboard, with a central space between
them; five baskets each weighing around 32kg were jammed in towards the bow of the boat, where they
were reasonably restricted from moving. JCK was known to have a regular bow trim; this and additional
catch weight stowed forward would have restricted her bow from rising to oncoming seas, thus increasing
the potential from swamping over the bow. Bold Venture’s construction of side chambers and thwarts
(Figure 7) enabled cargo to be reasonably well secured, thus limiting its freedom to move. Greater
space within the hull of JCK might have allowed the stowed catch to move, and also greater free surface
movement of accumulated sea water. Soon after clearing Thatcher Rock, Andrew was seen re-arranging
his boxes, confirming that the catch had almost certainly moved position during the initial passage.
When the skippers stopped the boats to enable them to bail and re-arrange stowage a few hundred
yards clear of Thatcher Rock, the passage had already been extremely hazardous, with the worst part
yet to come. This could have been an opportunity to jettison the catch to lighten the boats. Although
it is understandable how commercial pressures might have prevented such a consideration, jettisoning
would have improved the boats’ sea-keeping capabilities and should not have been ignored in such a life
threatening situation.
Loss of life
The skippers recognised that the 4 mile passage to Torquay would be hazardous, yet neither donned an
inflatable lifejacket. While there is an argument that some PFDs may be obstructive when hauling fishing
gear, it is of great concern that wearing them during sea passages was not customary on board JCK or
Bold Venture. Had Andrew worn his lifejacket, it would have not only increased his survival time in the
sea but would also have assisted his searchers to locate him more easily in the darkness. Andrew’s
survival time would have been even more significantly improved if he had been wearing his thermal
flotation suit (which he sometimes wore for warmth) along with an inflatable lifejacket; unfortunately he
did not put it on before sailing that day, possibly due to it being too warm when hauling nets.
13
It has been recognised for some time that many fishermen are reluctant to wear PFDs; indeed it has
been the focus of previous MAIB recommendations to the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) that
their wearing should be compulsory on open decks. The MCA is currently monitoring the success of
educational campaigns promoting the use and effectiveness of PFDs. If, by the start of 2015, it is found
that their use is not more widespread than at present, or MOB7 survival statistics have not improved,
regulation may then be introduced to make the wearing of PFDs mandatory on the open decks of fishing
vessels.
Neither vessel was equipped with an EPIRB or any other type of automatic distress signalling device.
Had JCK been fitted with a functioning EPIRB, it is likely that the alarm would have been raised
automatically up to 1 hour earlier than the call to the coastguard at 1853. The mandatory carriage of
EPIRBs on all fishing vessels has been the subject of MAIB recommendations to the MCA since 2008.
Since Andrew was not wearing a PFD, it cannot be stated that an EPIRB would have saved his life, but it
is clear that his chances of survival would have been improved.
Communications
On the day of the accident, despite the requirements in MSN 1813, neither JCK nor Bold Venture was
equipped with a working radio, as both vessels’ radios had malfunctioned and been left ashore. Both
skippers carried mobile telephones as a means of communicating with third parties. Andrew’s mobile
telephone went off the air at 1650, presumably due either to low battery power or water ingress, leaving
him unable to communicate remotely with others.
Mobile telephones are no substitute for marine radio; their transmissions are private, which prevents
emergency calls from being overheard by potential helpers; SAR assets are unable to use direction
finding equipment on their transmissions; they are not as easy to use as a radio in an emergency; and
their signals are more likely to be lost if base stations are obscured by cliffs or land masses.
The lack of radios prevented the skippers from obtaining weather updates, which are transmitted
regularly by the coastguard. More crucially, this prevented the skippers of JCK and Bold Venture from
drawing the coastguard’s attention to their distress8 situation. It is doubtful, however, if either skipper
would have asked for assistance, for fear of sparking a false alert. This is confirmed by the reluctance of
both Bold Venture’s skipper and Andrew’s father to contact the coastguard for over 40 minutes after Bold
Venture was safely back in port. Instead, they chose to carry out their own search from ashore. In such
situations and severe weather conditions the coastguard should be notified as soon as possible – better
a false alert than delaying potential rescue.
7 MOB: man overboard
8 Distress: grave and imminent danger.
14
CONCLUSIONS
• The full potential of Babbacombe’s sheltered bay and pier, if considered, was not taken advantage of.
• Weather forecasts were not properly evaluated, and contingencies for aborting the operation and
passage were not adequately considered.
• JCK foundered in severe weather conditions, in which heavily laden, 6.45m open decked boats should
not have been attempting a passage, especially in darkness.
• JCK’s inherent buoyancy was impaired.
• JCK was heavily laden with catch and equipment, with catch stowed in such a way that it trimmed the
vessel by the head. In severe conditions, such loading would have impaired the boat’s ability to rise to
oncoming seas and reduced her overall sea-keeping ability.
• Neither skipper chose to wear their inflatable lifejackets despite being aware of the hazardous
conditions to be encountered on passage.
• The decision to continue beyond Hope’s Nose towards Torquay was a severe error of judgment by the
skippers of both JCK and Bold Venture.
• EPIRBs were not carried or required.
• Neither vessel carried a working VHF radio. This prevented the skippers from obtaining weather
updates and from alerting the coastguard when they were in a distress situation.
• There was a delay in notifying the coastguard of JCK’s predicament.
RECOMMENDATIONS
No recommendations have been issued as a consequence of this investigation. However, the
circumstances of this tragic accident should serve as a warning to all mariners on the dangers of
proceeding to sea in vessels that are unsuited or ill prepared for the prevailing sea and weather
conditions.
Safety recommendations shall in no case create a presumption of blame or liability
15

Location: 0.5 nautical miles south-east of Porticello, Italy.

Accident Investigation Report 22/2026
Read our marine accident investigation report, which includes what happened, subsequent actions taken and recommendations.
MAIB investigation report 22-2026: Bayesian
The foundering of the sailing yacht Bayesian: MAIB’s investigation summary
Summary
At 0406 on 19 August 2024, the private sailing yacht Bayesian was at anchor 0.5 nautical miles south-east of Porticello, Italy. A violent downburst of hurricane-force winds knocked the vessel onto its starboard side. Unable to right itself, Bayesian flooded and sank in 50m of water. Six guests and one crew member died in the accident. None of the liferafts on board automatically inflated or released from the vessel, requiring the crew to do so manually. The crew organised the survivors in the water and assisted them into a liferaft. They were later rescued by a nearby vessel and then taken ashore.
Safety issues
The investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian was vulnerable to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle and the position of the centreboard, but had not been identified in the originally approved stability information available to the crew.
Information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather forecast for the area, while predominantly correct, did not indicate the risk of downbursts from the thunderstorms predicted.
Statement from the Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents
Recommendations
The Red Ensign Group is recommended to undertake a study of the vulnerabilities identified in this report and amend the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code and associated guidance to account for its findings.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is recommended to amend its training syllabus for yacht masters to include the risks from downbursts and severe wind gusts.
The Met Office is recommended to raise with the World Meteorological Organization the need to consider how low likelihood, high impact weather hazards should be represented in its data services.
The UK Hydrographic Office is recommended to develop and update guidance on the risks of such extreme weather in its publications.
Related publications

safety flyer to the yachting industry
has been produced with this report.

SYNOPSIS
At 0406 on 19 August 2024, the private sailing yacht
Bayesian was at anchor 0.5 nautical miles south-east of
Porticello, Italy. A violent downburst of hurricane-force
winds knocked the vessel onto its starboard side. Unable
to right itself, Bayesian flooded and sank in 50m of water.
Six guests and nine crew members escaped the vessel
as it foundered. Six guests and one crew member died in
Italy
the accident. None of the liferafts on board automatically
inflated or released from the vessel, requiring the crew to
do so manually. The crew organised the survivors in the
water and assisted them into a liferaft. They were later
rescued by a nearby vessel and then taken ashore.
The investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian’s
windage and stability characteristics left it vulnerable Sicily
to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was
affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle
and the position of the centreboard, but had not been
identified in the originally approved stability information
available to the crew.
Information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail
of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather
forecast for the area, while predominantly correct, did not indicate the risk of downbursts
from the thunderstorms predicted.
Following the accident the MAIB published an interim report and has prepared a paper to
submit to the International Maritime Organization to highlight the investigation findings.
Recommendations have been made to the Red Ensign Group to undertake a study of the
vulnerabilities identified in this report and amend the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code and
associated guidance to account for its findings.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency has been recommended to amend its training
syllabus for yacht masters to include the risks from downbursts and severe wind gusts.
A recommendation has also been made to the UK Met Office to raise with the World
Meteorological Organization the need to consider how low likelihood, high impact weather
hazards should be represented in its data services.
Lastly a recommendation has been made to the UK Hydrographic Office to develop and
update guidance on the risks of such extreme weather in its publications.

1.2 BACKGROUND
Bayesian (Figure 1) was a 55.9m monohull sloop1 with a beam of 11.5m and a
hollow aluminium mast that stood 72.25m above the waterline. The yacht (Figure 2)
had three decks and a flying bridge with guest and crew cabins below the main
deck. The yacht’s machinery spaces, service and crew areas were located forward
and aft of the guest cabins. Internal access routes led up through the saloon,
wheelhouse and flying bridge. Bayesian had a hydraulic retractable centreboard.
Bayesian was operated as a private pleasure vessel. It regularly spent summers
cruising in the Mediterranean Sea.

1.3 INVESTIGATION SCOPE
Following the accident the Italian public prosecutor launched a criminal investigation
in Termini Imerese, Sicily. Consequently, MAIB access to some witnesses and
to evidence held by the public prosecutor was restricted. It is possible that the
circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence
withheld by the Italian authorities.
This report does not examine the Italian authorities’ search and rescue response
or the circumstances surrounding the death of a diver during the operation to
salvage Bayesian.
1.4 NARRATIVE
On 14 August 2024, Bayesian sailed from the port of Milazzo, Italy for an excursion
around the Aeolian Islands and the north coast of Sicily. There were 12 guests and
10 crew on board. The intention was to disembark the guests on 19 August before
proceeding to Naples for maintenance. On the morning of 18 August, Bayesian was
anchored at Cefalù, northern Sicily.
With the weather forecast indicating an increasing westerly wind, the master decided
to motor towards Porticello, 25 nautical miles (nm) to the west, and anchor overnight.
The anchorage at Porticello afforded shelter from the forecast winds and allowed
for easy disembarkation of guests the following day. At 2124, Bayesian anchored
to the east of the main breakwater. Its centreboard was raised. The sailing vessel
Sir Robert Baden Powell2 was also at anchor close by.
Thunderstorms had been forecast, and occasional flashes of lightning to the west
were seen from on board. The master checked the latest weather forecast and
retired for the night, leaving instructions for the overnight watchkeepers (deckhands
DH1 and DH2) to wake them if the wind increased above 20 knots (kts) or if there
were signs that the anchor was dragging. DH1 and the evening steward (S1) were
on duty.
By 0030 on 19 August 2024, the last guest had gone to bed. At 0100, DH2 took over
the watch from DH1. The wind was noted as being no more than 8kts and there
were no indications that Bayesian was dragging its anchor.
1.4.1 The accident
At 0300, DH2 noted that the wind was still 8kts from the west but thought that
thunderclouds and lightning visible in the distance seemed to be getting closer. At
about 0330, two of the guests (G1 and G2) woke but remained resting in their cabin.
At about 0330, the master of Sir Robert Baden Powell went on deck to oversee
the transfer of guests ashore in the vessel’s tender. Seeing the approaching
thunderstorms, the master decided to delay disembarking their guests and ready the
engine for manoeuvring.
On board Bayesian, DH2 also noted the advancing thunderstorm and checked the
weather forecast on their personal device before videoing it. At 0344, they posted
the video on social media. They then went on deck and closed three hatches on the

The C/O returned to the flying bridge and briefed the master on the crew activities.
The master then told the C/O to check if the C/E had started the engines and pumps
so that they could manoeuvre Bayesian into the wind. The C/O descended to the
wheelhouse, where the C/E informed them that Bayesian was ready to manoeuvre.
The C/O shouted up to the flying bridge to let the master know.
The owner, G3, and G4 (carrying G5) arrived in the saloon as the rain-soaked CS
came in from the upper deck with items they wanted to protect from the rain and
strengthening wind.
As the master prepared to manoeuvre Bayesian, the wind suddenly increased to
about 70kts. The awning over the flying bridge ripped from port to starboard. At
0406, Bayesian violently heeled over 90° to starboard, taking less than 15 seconds
to do so. People, furniture and loose items fell across the deck. The generators shut
down immediately and battery-supplied emergency lighting automatically turned on.
The master, G4, owner, bosun and steward 2 (S2) were all injured, either by falling,
or from items falling on them as Bayesian rolled onto its side. DH2 had been thrown
into the sea from their position on the flying bridge and climbed back on board.
In their cabin, guests G1 and G2 used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder
to exit into the central alleyway. They climbed along the internal walls, making
their way up the staircase into the saloon. S1 and DH1 climbed up the walls of the
forward crew staircase, exiting from the crew mess area into the wheelhouse.
There was no indication of flooding inside Bayesian until water came in over the
starboard rails as the yacht heeled over. With Bayesian lying on its side, water
entered the internal spaces down the stairwells and into the accommodation.
The C/E exited the wheelhouse through the port forward wheelhouse door. Once
clear, they helped DH1 out before moving to the yacht’s port aft quarter where an
emergency position-indicating radio beacon (EPIRB) was located. DH1 remained
outside the wheelhouse door. Reaching down through the door, DH1 lifted both S1
and S2 out of the wheelhouse. With no one else immediately visible, the three crew
members went aft and into the sea.
Separately, the C/O found the owner in the saloon and pushed them to the master
on the flying bridge through the cascading water. The C/O and master evacuated
G3, G4 and G5 by the same route.
Guests G1 and G2 went forward and into the wheelhouse. The bosun and DH2
assisted them onto the flying bridge.
As Bayesian rotated further to starboard and started to sink, the CS, bosun and DH2
were in a diminishing air pocket in the wheelhouse by the now closed port forward
wheelhouse door. Assisted from outside by the injured G4, the three crew members
opened the door and escaped.
The C/O had attempted to ascend to the flying bridge but was unable to due to the
force of the water coming down. They were swept to an air pocket at the back of the
saloon. They dived down and, after several attempts, opened the sliding doors at the
rear of the space and swam clear.
9
The master instructed the guests on the flying bridge to swim away from the yacht
and warned them to remain clear of the mast and boom as Bayesian was sinking.
At about 0412, the C/E deployed the EPIRB and then sat on the hull near the rudder.
The C/E noted that the wind had eased and that Bayesian was only a short distance
from shore. Hearing shouts from the master, the C/E jumped into the sea and swam
towards the survivors gathering in the water.
The CS counted those present and checked for injuries. DH2 improvised a
tourniquet for G4’s gashed arm and G2 gathered a cushion to use as a flotation
device for G5. Guest G1 used the torch on their mobile phone to search the water
for other survivors.
The master and DH1 swam back to Bayesian. They unsuccessfully tried to release
the port aft liferaft from its stowage. The C/O swam to the port forward liferaft.
Releasing it from its stowage, the C/O towed the canister to the gathered survivors.
By about 0424, the liferaft was inflated and DH1 entered it and helped the survivors
to board.
From their position in the liferaft, the CS saw the bows of Bayesian rise up and then
sink below the surface. The crew administered first aid to the injured and gathered
the means to raise the alarm from the equipment contained in the liferaft. One of the
survivors recalled seeing a vortex of water between the clouds and the sea surface
a short distance away.
Bayesian sank in approximately 50m of water.
1.4.2 The rescue
The master of Sir Robert Baden Powell noted that the vessel had dragged its anchor
over 350m in 11 minutes. Bayesian was not visible and the crew of Sir Robert Baden
Powell initially believed that Bayesian had left the anchorage to avoid the sudden
storm. The master of Sir Robert Baden Powell briefly saw a dark triangular shape in
the water.
At 0434, Bayesian’s C/E fired a red parachute flare from the liferaft. As it rose, the
flare was carried sideways in an area of strong wind. The C/E used the torch from
the liferaft to signal towards the shore and to Sir Robert Baden Powell. At 0443, the
C/E fired a second red parachute flare. The crew on board Sir Robert Baden Powell
responded to the flares and the vessel’s master dispatched its tender to assist,
heading towards the visible flashing lights on the EPIRB and liferaft.
On arrival at the liferaft, Sir Robert Baden Powell’s tender crew transferred
the survivors on board. One of the survivors noted a cone shape in the sky
and estimated it to be about 100m in diameter, rising into the clouds above. At
0453, after a brief search for other survivors, the tender returned to Sir Robert
Baden Powell.
The tender crew transferred the survivors to Sir Robert Baden Powell and,
accompanied by Bayesian’s C/E, returned to the accident site to search for others.
The tender returned to Sir Robert Baden Powell about 20 minutes later. At 0520,
10
Sir Robert Baden Powell’s master called the local coastguard to report the accident
and arrange transfers ashore. Accompanied by Bayesian’s master, the tender crew
conducted a third and final search for survivors.
Over the next hour, all survivors were taken ashore for medical treatment and
reception by the local authorities.

1.6 ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS
The sea surface temperature at the time of the accident was about 31°C. Winds
immediately before and after the accident were north-westerly, Beaufort force 3 to 5.
The weather is discussed in more detail in section 1.11 of this report.
1.7 BAYESIAN
1.7.1 General
Bayesian was built by Perini Navi S.p.A (Perini Navi) in 2008. Originally registered
as Salute in the Netherlands, it was the was only sloop of this size constructed by
Perini Navi; the other yachts were built as ketches6. In 2014, the owner at the time of
the accident acquired the yacht through Revtom Ltd and its name was changed to
Bayesian, registered in the UK.
Bayesian’s single mast was hollow, though closed at its top, and had six pairs
of spreaders up it. The regularly spaced spreaders were raked backwards and
decreased in size up the mast. At the lowest spreader, the mast was 570mm wide.
The 22m boom contained the mainsail when furled and was suspended aft of
the mast. Forward of the mast there was a 12m spar that was used to move the
yacht’s boats.
There were three main stairways up from the crew accommodation, leading to a
hatch on the foredeck, the forward guest cockpit, and the wheelhouse respectively
(see Figure 2). The wheelhouse stairway was mainly used by crew but could also
be accessed as a secondary escape from the guest accommodation. The stairway
leading up into the saloon from just forward of the owner’s cabin was the main route
to and from the guest accommodation and served as the primary escape route.
Internally, access to the flying bridge was via a stairway from the wheelhouse.
Access to the lazarette, engine room and engineer’s cabin was through a hatch on
the port side of the main deck that led to a stairway into the lazarette. There were
three doors on the main deck: one either side of the wheelhouse, opening outwards
into the forward guest cockpit, and a set of sliding doors at the aft end of the saloon
leading into the aft guest cockpit.
Guest cabins were arranged around a central corridor with doors opening inwards
into each of the six cabin spaces.
Window shutters were available on board. At the time of the accident these were
not fitted.
1.7.2 Tanks and machinery installation
Bayesian had tanks for fresh water, lubricating oil fuel oil, sewage, bilge water and
oil sludge. Each evening the C/E filled the fuel oil day tanks. Generally, fuel oil was
drawn from the aft fuel storage tanks in preference to the forward tanks to manage
Bayesian’s trim and maintain the machinery exhausts clear of the waterline.

On 19 August 2024, the fuel level in two of the aft fuel oil storage tanks was low in
preparation for the upcoming maintenance period. The yacht’s fresh water tanks
were generally maintained full, although the water makers were routinely switched
off at about 1900 to minimise noise overnight.
For propulsion, Bayesian had two 720kW diesel engines driving two controllable
pitch propellers. Three 90kW generators provided the main electrical power supply.
For emergency power, a 20kW emergency generator was installed in a compartment
below the forward deck and there was also a 24V battery bank.
Bayesian could be controlled and navigated from either the wheelhouse or the
flying bridge. The propulsion machinery could be controlled from either the engine
control room, wheelhouse or flying bridge. It was the practice on board to follow the
operating manual and to start and stop main engines from the engine control room.
Control was then transferred to either the wheelhouse or flying bridge as required.
Engine room ventilation supply and extraction ducts were fitted with watertight
anti-flood shutters. Those for the ventilation supply were manually operated and
those for the extraction were remotely controlled. The shutters on each side of
the yacht could also be closed independently when necessary, depending on the
operating conditions. The engines were each fitted with a water-cooled exhaust
that injected seawater into the exhaust stream to both cool the exhaust and reduce
noise. Valves in the exhaust systems were required to be opened for the engines to
start and run.
Closing devices on hull openings had not been manually operated at the time of the
accident (see section 1.8.2).
1.7.3 Keel and centreboard
Bayesian had a fixed box keel structure extending below its hull. The box keel was
filled with 41.31 tonnes (t) of lead ballast. The box keel gave Bayesian a design
draught of 4.05m.
A deployable centreboard filled with 52.3t of lead ballast was set into a housing in
the box keel. Once lowered, the centreboard increased the yacht’s draught to 9.83m.
The centreboard could be raised and lowered hydraulically. It took approximately
2 minutes and 30 seconds to deploy the centreboard using both the associated
hydraulic pumps. Recovery of the centreboard took approximately 3 minutes and
40 seconds. The crew were aware of the increased draught when the centreboard
was in the lowered position. When raised, the centreboard was secured in place by
a hydraulic lock when the hydraulic pumps were switched off.
The centreboard was designed for use when the yacht was in the sailing condition.
It was not required when Bayesian was motoring with its sails down.
1.7.4 Crew
Bayesian had 10 permanent crew. The master, C/O and CS had all been on board
Bayesian for over 3 months at the time of the accident. The C/E, bosun, chef,
stewards and DH1 had all been on board for about 2 months. DH2 had been on
board for about a month. Each crew member undertook familiarisation training when

they joined the vessel. The working language on board was English, which all the

The master had captained Bayesian since early 2022 and had over 23 years’

The C/O had 8 years’ seafaring experience, of which they had served 2 years on

The C/E had 13 years’ experience on board Bayesian. The chef had over 25 years’

The CS had a background in hospitality and had served on board Bayesian since

500gt. S1 and S2 were new to Bayesian in 2024; both had completed the relevant

The bosun had started working on private yachts in 2011 and qualified as an
offshore yachtmaster in 2020. They had served on board Bayesian since 2022.
Both DH1 and DH2 had joined Bayesian for the first time at the start of the 2024
summer season. Both DH1 and DH2 had completed the relevant basic training.
Additionally, DH2 held a yachtmaster offshore certificate of competency.
1.7.5 Guests
There were 12 guests on board Bayesian, including the owner and their family who
were familiar with the vessel.
On joining Bayesian, short safety briefings were given to those who had not sailed
on the yacht before. Separate safety briefings were delivered by the C/O before
Bayesian went under sail, or when guests embarked via the tender.
The owner and Dr Mike Lynch were staying in the master cabin in the aft section
of the guest accommodation. Jonathan and Judy Bloomer were in the port side
forward cabin, G1 and G2 in the starboard side forward cabin, and Chris and Neda
Morvillo in the starboard side midships cabin. Guests G3, G4 and G5 were staying
in the port side midships cabin, and Hannah Lynch was staying in the port side aft
nanny’s cabin (see Figure 2).

1.7.6 Anchoring
Bayesian anchored at Porticello with 2.5 shackles (69m) of chain out on the port
anchor in 30m of water. Bayesian carried 150m of chain on each side connected to
stockless anchors.
On 22 July 2024, Bayesian had been anchored in the Bay of Naples. During a
period of high wind, the yacht had started to drag its port anchor, as had other
superyachts anchored in the same area. During that event, the crew used the
engines and the bow thruster to minimise the drag. Bayesian had reportedly heeled
over to approximately 15°.
Bayesian had a propensity to yaw8 at anchor when the centreboard was lowered.
This increased snatching on the anchor cable and the consequential dragging risk.
Excessive yaw also caused discomfort for those on board. The centreboard was
rarely lowered when Bayesian was at anchor.
1.7.7 Lifesaving equipment
Bayesian carried four 12-person liferafts on the bridge deck (see Figure 2): two on
the forward deck, and two aft of the aft guest cockpit. Each liferaft sat in a hinged
cradle designed to allow each liferaft to float free should the yacht sink in an upright
condition. The cradles could be operated manually by the crew to deploy the liferafts
as part of a controlled abandonment.
During Bayesian’s salvage the two aft liferafts were dislodged and floated free of the
wreck and then inflated. The forward starboard liferaft remained in position and was
recovered with the vessel (Figure 5). Each hydrostatic release unit (HRU), intended
to release the liferafts from their cradles in the event of the vessel sinking, had
operated as designed.

1.7.8 Vessel certification
When built in 2008, Bayesian (then Salute), was surveyed against the requirements
of the UK Large Commercial Yacht Code (LY2)9. The MCA issued a certificate of
compliance against the LY2 requirements. When Salute became Bayesian in 2014,
it was operated privately and was not available for chartering or other commercial
activities and was therefore not required to comply with the requirements of LY2.
No survey or certification activities related to compliance with LY2 was carried
out on the vessel after this date. However, it was maintained substantially to the
LY2 standard, including any subsequent amendments that would apply to a vessel
in commercial operation; no surveys were conducted to verify compliance with
the standard.
Bayesian was registered in the UK and was subject to the requirements for survey
and certification as a pleasure vessel. The certification requirements were set out in
MGN 599 (M)10 published by the MCA in 2019. The yacht was subject to statutory
and Class surveys carried out by surveyors from the American Bureau of Shipping
(ABS). None of the statutory surveys required for Bayesian required an assessment
of its stability.
1.7.9 Yacht management
In November 2014, the owner of Bayesian engaged Camper and Nicholsons
International Limited (CNI) to manage the yacht’s survey and maintenance activities.
All guest arrangements were made by the owner directly.
As a privately operated vessel, Bayesian was not required to implement a safety
management system. However, it operated a voluntary safety management system
based on the requirements annexed to LY2 and informed by CNI’s Mini-ISM system.
The responsibility for the management of Bayesian fell to a subsidiary of CNI
based in Monaco. The fleet managers would regularly attend the vessel during
maintenance periods and were in routine contact with the crew to offer guidance
and support as required. The assigned fleet managers had worked with Bayesian for
several years and were familiar with the yacht and its crew.
1.7.10 On board documentation
Operational documents and certificates were kept in Bayesian’s wheelhouse.
These included the vessel’s Operations and Safety Manual, Mini-ISM system,
standing orders, and operational procedures and checklists. Bayesian also carried

1.7.11 Wreck examination
Limited information was provided to the investigation on the recovery operations
carried out on Bayesian. Although some dive videos were available, no dive records
were provided that detailed the activities undertaken during the initial dives to
recover the casualties.
The information available showed that Bayesian was lying on its starboard side on
the seabed. The centreboard was in the raised position, and the transom shell door
was closed.
The trace of the anchor scouring on the seabed mirrored the track of Bayesian
shown in Figure 4.
The wreck of Bayesian was recovered to Termini Imerese, Sicily in June 2025. The
MAIB was denied immediate access to the wreck by the Italian authorities. In July
2025, MAIB inspectors completed an external laser scan of the hull of the vessel
to support the stability study. Examination of the yacht’s internal spaces was not
allowed at that time.
The Italian authorities permitted access to Bayesian in December 2025. When
inspected, the yacht’s internal spaces had been cleared of debris. Furniture, fittings,
equipment and stores had been removed. No documented record of the items
removed was available.
1.8 STABILITY INFORMATION
1.8.1 General
Bayesian was provided with a stability information booklet (SIB) which described
the stability characteristics of the yacht in the intact condition. The SIB detailed
the arrangements of Bayesian’s sails, hatches, doors and openings as well as
tank information.
Bayesian’s SIB had been assessed against the requirements of LY2 by Ensign large
yacht services11 and was approved on 3 July 2008.
Bayesian was subject to a voluntary lightship check12 conducted on 12 November
2020. The derived values were compared with those from the original stability
assessment carried out in 2008, which were included in the SIB. The increase in
lightship weight was 0.19% and the position of the longitudinal centre of gravity had
moved aft by 0.60%.
11 Ensign large yacht services was a specialist unit within the MCA. Ensign surveyors completed survey and

1.8.2 Downflooding
Downflooding is the entry of seawater into the hull of a vessel through a fixed
opening. It occurs once the relevant opening is immersed by water. The SIB stated
that critical flooding would occur when openings with an aggregate area greater than
0.377m² were submerged13.
The SIB set out the angle of heel where downflooding would occur in the three
arrival and departure conditions with the centreboard in both the raised and lowered
conditions. In the light load motoring condition, downflooding would start at 34.3°
of heel and become critical at 47.5° when engine room ventilation and extraction
openings were submerged. The identified openings and associated downflooding
angles for Bayesian in various approved conditions are set out in Table 214.

1.8.3 Guidance on the prevention of capsize
The SIB template published by the MCA noted the need for a section outlining
guidance to the master on shipboard procedures. It stated that the SIB
should include:
any procedures relating to the safe operation of the yacht affecting stability or
survivability following damage, hit by squalls etc that the master is to be made
aware of in order that the appropriate action can be taken either in the course of
normal seagoing preparation or in the case of an emergency
The template provided generic suggested text, noting that it was not to be
considered exhaustive of what is expected and that they should be modified as
required to suite the specific yacht in question [sic]. The guidance in the SIB on
Bayesian mirrored the generic text from the template.
The SIB on Bayesian detailed precautions to be taken to prevent capsize while it
was underway, including that the master should:
exercise prudence and good seamanship having regard. [sic] to the season of
the year, experience of the crew, weather forecast and the navigational zone,
and should take appropriate action as to the speed, course and sail setting
warranted by the prevailing conditions.
The SIB noted that:
The amount of sail carried is at the discretion of the Master and his decision will
have to take into account many factors.
Further, that:
The Master should note that the presence of the vent and skylights significantly
reduces the ability of the vessel to withstand down flooding and with these
openings securely closed the safety of the vessel is enhanced considerably.
The SIB identified the risk of capsize in gusts or squalls, advising the master to use
the readings from the inclinometer and anemometer to determine the risk. It stated
that the master may then:
decide to shorten sail together with other actions he considers necessary.
The SIB discussed precautions to be taken against the risk of capsize, including
that all external hull doors and flush hatches were to be closed and secured, and
stated that:
In adverse weather conditions and where there is the possibility of encountering
a severe gust, squall or large breaking wave, all exposed doors, hatches,
skylights, vents, etc. should be closed and securely fastened to prevent the
ingress of water. If available, storm boards, blanking plates etc. should be
erected and fitted.
20
The SIB’s ‘Master shipboard procedures’ section considered four scenarios:
1. In sheltered anchorages and in port – reminding masters of their responsibilities
to evaluate risks and hazards and take appropriate precautions. The SIB
recommended that the door from the lazarette to the engine room be kept closed
whenever the shell door was open.
2. Preparing for sea – all external hull doors and flush hatches, internal hinged
watertight doors and sidelights that could be opened were to be closed securely.
Internal sliding watertight doors had to be tested.
3. Preparing for rough weather passage – reminding masters of their responsibility
to take precautions, including, but not be limited to, securely lashing all loose gear,
large or heavy items of furniture, putting shutters over the windows, and to secure
closing device as appropriate.
4. At sea – the internal sliding watertight doors could be left open when appropriate
but should be checked as required to make sure they closed properly. Internal
hinged watertight doors should remain closed but may be opened when passing
trough [sic].
Bayesian’s Operation and Safety Manual included checklists for preparing for sea
and entering heavy weather. The checklists mirrored the advice provided in the SIB
for the closing of watertight hatches, doors and hull openings.
The SIB’s ‘Master responsibility on stability under sail’ section highlighted that the
angle of vanishing stability (or GZ righting lever positive range)17 was 84.3° when
Bayesian was in the light load sailing condition with the centreboard lowered.
The SIB contained graphs of statical stability (GZ curves) for maximum load,
contractual full load and light load conditions when in the sailing condition
(centreboard lowered and with sails set). A GZ curve describes a vessel’s ability to
return to an upright position. The gust limit is defined by the point at which the wind
heeling forces are balanced by a vessel’s capacity to right itself or the point at which
a vessel reaches an angle of heel sufficient to commence critical downflooding (or
60°, whichever is the lesser value). Beyond that limit, should the wind heeling forces
be sustained, the vessel would be knocked down or subject to critical downflooding.
Beyond the angle of vanishing stability, a vessel is no longer able to right itself
irrespective of any wind heeling forces.
The steady state wind heeling curve is derived from the gust wind heeling curve. At
any angle, the value of the steady state wind heeling lever is half of the gust wind
heeling lever. The steady state wind heeling limit is then defined as the point at
which the steady state wind heeling curve first intersects the GZ curve. Beyond the
steady state wind heeling limit a vessel is considered to be at risk of knockdown or
downflooding as the result of a wind gust. In the light load condition, when under
sail and with the centreboard down, the SIB detailed Bayesian’s steady state wind
heeling limit as 17.0°.
17 The angle of vanishing stability is the angle of heel where the righting moment has reached zero and is no
longer able to right itself. The GZ righting lever positive range describes the range from upright (0°) to the
angle of vanishing stability.
21
1.8.4 Management of wind heeling moment
The SIB detailed the respective curves of maximum steady heel angle to prevent
downflooding in gusts and squalls. These sections were provided for Bayesian in
specific sailing conditions, all with the centreboard lowered. This information was not
provided for any motoring conditions with the centreboard raised and no sails set.
Bayesian had an automatic sail monitoring and control system that was used to
control the sails when the yacht was under sail. This system monitored the sail
operating loads and would automatically ease the sheets to reduce the wind heeling
moment when preset load limits were surpassed.
1.9 WOLFSON UNIT STABILITY STUDIES
1.9.1 Initial stability and windage study
Following the accident, the MAIB contracted the University of Southampton’s
Wolfson Unit for Marine Technology and Industrial Aerodynamics (Wolfson Unit) to
conduct a stability and windage study of Bayesian.
The Wolfson Unit’s initial study considered the stability information available for the
yacht, including the original approved SIB, the MCA digital stability model used for
the original assessment and approval of its stability information, and drawings from
Bayesian’s builders.
The study assessed an assumed loss condition equating to the light load motoring
condition with the centreboard raised. The results of this study (Annex A) were used
to inform the MAIB’s interim report (Annex D) published in May 2025.
The initial study identified inconsistencies between the stability model used when
the SIB was originally approved and the other documents contributing to the study.
These were addressed in the development of the digital stability model by the
Wolfson Unit, which was subsequently used to calculate the vessel’s stability. The
report of the study stated that:
Even though differences have been observed between the SIB and the Wolfson
models, these had no significant impact on the overall stability characteristics of
the vessel at the loading conditions evaluated.
The Wolfson Unit study also assessed Bayesian’s aerodynamic loading with no sails
set to estimate the maximum wind speed that the yacht could withstand given its
stability characteristics. The study concluded that, With the wind on the beam and
the vessel in the motoring light load condition…an envelope of limiting wind speed of
53 – 63 knots could capsize the vessel.
1.9.2 Post-wreck examination study
The Wolfson Unit was subsequently contracted to refine its initial assessment
of Bayesian’s stability characteristics and aerodynamic loading based on the
information recovered once the wreck was brought ashore. Estimates of tank
contents and stores were based on information gathered during the investigation
and details of the yacht’s intended operation. This work was completed in March
2026 (Annex B).
22
The Wolfson Unit study used the data from the laser scan of the hull conducted
during the investigation and updated the initial stability and aerodynamic models to
account for tank contents, deadweight assessments, and the aerodynamic effects of
the yacht’s fittings. The study also assessed the possible impact of accumulation of
rainwater in the lazarette.
The probable loss condition assessed was based on the best information available
but remains an estimate of Bayesian’s stability condition when the yacht foundered.
The Wolfson Unit derived wind heeling data for Bayesian in the probable loss
condition (Figure 6). The aerodynamic study predicted the wind speeds that would
produce the limiting heel angle for apparent wind angle (AWA) ranges relative to the
bows. These predictions are shown in Table 3. The predicted high limits included
the impact of interactions and blanketing effects between different elements of the
mast and rigging. The predicted low limits excluded these effects.
In the probable loss condition, the Wolfson Unit study concluded that Bayesian
would maintain a positive righting lever when heeled over until the angle of heel
reached 73° – the angle of vanishing stability. The derived wind heeling moment in
this condition indicated that the vessel was at risk from gusts when at a steady wind
heeling angle of 13.9° (Figure 6).
The Wolfson Unit assessed that Bayesian’s mast contributed more than 56% of the
total wind heeling moment and the furled sails contributed more than another 20%.
The study concluded that accumulated rainwater in the lazarette was unlikely to
have been a significant factor.

1.10 ABANDON SHIP PROCESS AND DRILLS
Bayesian’s Operation and Safety Manual included information on the alarm signals
and actions to be taken in the event of the need to abandon ship. A muster list
assigned tasks to the crew for the mustering of people and the process for a
controlled abandonment of Bayesian.
The guests were to muster in the aft guest cockpit and await instructions during any
emergency on board.
Bayesian’s crew completed monthly training on emergency procedures, although not
normally when guests were on board.
1.11 ACCESS TO WEATHER INFORMATION
Bayesian was equipped with a digital navigational telex (NAVTEX)18 unit in the
wheelhouse that displayed marine safety information provided by an authorised
provider, including navigational warnings and search and rescue information.
Additionally, it provided meteorological forecasts and warnings.
18 An international automated direct printing telex system that was an integral part of the Global Maritime
Distress and Safety System and the Worldwide Met-Ocean Information and Warning Service (WWMIWS).
24
Meteorological weather forecasts sent via NAVTEX were transmitted in a specific
timeslot. These were locally transmitted to ensure relevance to the vessel receiving
the signal, although local stations needed to have been selected on the receiving
unit. Weather forecasts were broadcast at least twice daily and were coordinated
across the meteorological area (MetArea).
The authorised provider could use NAVTEX to set off an alarm at the receiving unit,
alerting vessels to important warnings. Meteorological warnings were allocated a
priority of ‘important’ and were repeated at each subsequent scheduled transmission
for as long as the warning was in force. Such warnings only contained the warning
information and were separate to the weather forecast.
The NAVTEX unit on Bayesian was operational in the period leading up to the
accident. The crew routinely referred to official forecasts and warnings received by
this method.
The guidance in MGN 599 (M) strongly advised crews on board pleasure vessels
to check the weather and tidal conditions. The crew supplemented NAVTEX
information with both official and unofficial data from application-based programs
available on their smartphones. The master referred to such application-based
programs regularly.
1.12 WEATHER AND CLIMATE
1.12.1 General conditions
On the evening of 18 August 2024, the predominant winds off Sicily’s north coast
were forecast to be from the north-west at between force 3 or 4, gusting up to force
5 or 6. An area of low pressure that was moving in a south-easterly direction from
the Gulf of Genoa towards the north Tyrrhenian Sea. This area of low pressure
deepened as it developed. Another area of low pressure had developed during the
day in the Tyrrhenian Sea and was moving slowly towards Sicily’s north coast.
As the evening progressed, thunderstorms developed over the north Sicilian
coastline and there were regular bursts of lightning and heavy showers. The
photograph of Bayesian taken from Sir Robert Baden Powell 14 minutes before its
foundering showed how the weather appeared locally off the coast (see Figure 3).
Surface winds returned to a north-westerly force 3 or 4 following the accident.
1.12.2 Marine weather forecasts for the western Mediterranean Sea
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) divided the world’s oceans up into
21 different areas. The provision of marine meteorological information to shipping
was delivered by the WWMIWS, which was part of the WMO.
The Mediterranean Sea was designated as MetArea III and was coordinated by
Greece. Météo-France was responsible for the provision of forecasts and services
in the western Mediterranean Sea, covering the area from the west coast of Italy
to the Strait of Gibraltar. Figure 7 shows the geographic extent of the MetArea III
meteorological areas near the accident site.

1.12.4 Convective available potential energy
Convective available potential energy (CAPE), measured in joules per kg (J/kg),
describes the instability of the atmosphere and provides an approximation of updraft
strength within a thunderstorm. Higher CAPE values generally indicate there is more
energy in a system and greater potential for strong thunderstorms to form.
Theoretical virtual temperatures are used to account for the impact of moisture
on the air density through which an air parcel moves. Use of virtual temperatures
enables the production of more accurate estimates of CAPE, known as most
unstable CAPE (MUCAPE).
At 0200 and 1400 each day, weather balloon ascent data was recorded at
Trapani-Birgi Airport, Sicily, 59 miles west-south-west of the accident site. At 0200
on 19 August 2024, the airport recorded a surface air pressure of 1,009 hPa and
winds of 3kts from the west.
The ascent data from Trapani was used to derive an assessment of the CAPE in
the atmosphere. Using a virtual temperature, the MUCAPE was assessed to have a
value of 2,553.73 J/kg. Values of MUCAPE above 2,000 J/kg are indicative of strong
atmospheric instability with a high potential for severe convective weather.
1.12.5 Weather study
The MAIB commissioned the UK Met Office to conduct a study of the weather
conditions over the seas north of Sicily on the night of 18/19 August 2024.
The Met Office concluded that a trough approached northern Sicily through a region
characterised by a broad area of low pressure. Referencing the weather balloon
ascent at Trapani-Birgi Airport, the study stated that:
…the Trapani ascent suggests large amounts of CAPE available and shear28
borderline for supercell development29 (0-6km shear) and also borderline for
bow echoes30 or downdrafts (0-3km shear).
The Met Office noted that the Trapani observations were not directly within the
area of the most significant storm activity and that atmospheric instability and wind
shear may have been even greater nearer to the developing storm. High inshore
sea surface temperatures may also have contributed energy to the development of
weather systems.
The Met Office study of available satellite imagery concluded that:
a mesocyclonic storm front was probably demonstrating the properties of a
significant supercell. In this type of weather system, it is possible for associated
downdrafts to reach near-surface wind speeds up to, and exceptionally in excess
of, 100 miles per hour (87kts).
28 Changes to wind speed or direction with increasing altitude, or around local geographic features.
29 An isolated storm containing updrafts of vertically rotating wind (known as a mesocyclonic storm). Supercells
can produce damaging winds and develop into a tornado. Downdraft associated winds can be intense and
cause damage when they reach the ground.
30 A fast-moving system capable of producing extreme straight-line winds. Bow echoes develop when a strong,
organised squall line (or cluster of storms) begins to surge forward faster in the middle than at the ends.
30
The study further concluded that a mesocyclonic storm was highly likely, with an
associated supercell being probable. Further, the study suggested that tornadic
waterspouts and downdrafts were possible where local winds could reach extreme
hurricane force. The horizontal extent of such tornadic waterspout features could be
as small as 50m to 100m.
The Met Office noted that:
…with increasing sea surface temperatures and availability of moisture,
tornadoes in the Mediterranean might be increasing in the future climate, but
there is high uncertainty and low confidence in this notion…
1.12.6 Other meteorological studies
On 22 August 2024, the CNMCA produced a report into the meteorological
conditions at the time of the accident. This report studied satellite data and local
observations. The report stated that the nature of the weather and the lack of
available observation data did not allow a precise explanation.
On its examination of the data from Trapani-Birgi airport, the CNMCA report
stated that:
The thermodynamic survey carried out by the Trapani station at 00UTC shows a
very high CAPE1 index value of 3200 Joule/kg and also the presence of strong
DLS (Deep Layer Shear) windshear between 0-6 km (18 m/s). These values are
favourable for the formation of thunderstorms organised into supercells…
The report concluded that:
The meteorological event over Porticello is associated with the passage
of a thunderstorm line within the rapid transit of a cold frontal system. This
type of weather system is generally capable of producing strong, organised
thunderstorms over very large areas.
And that:
It is not possible to determine whether the event was a strong downburst (falling
winds associated with thunderstorm activity) or a waterspout… However, from
the information recorded by various meteorological stations along the coast, the
hypothesis of a strong downburst current seems more reasonable…
In November 2025, the Royal Meteorological Society journal Weather carried a
paper on the Bayesian accident31. The paper studied local observations from three
local CCTV cameras, the Trapani-Birgi Airport ascent data, available satellite
information, and data gathered from local amateur weather stations.
31 De Martin et al. (2025). The Bayesian sinking in Porticello: a predictable convective windstorm? RMetS
Weather, volume 80, No.11.
31
The paper concluded that the wind generated at the time of the accident was likely
to have been a downburst associated with a convective windstorm. The paper
further stated that:
While these observations suggest that the storm responsible may not have
been a supercell, in the absence of radar observations, we cannot be entirely
confident in this conclusion. While we are not aware of any tornado damage
along the coast, and all the observations analysed in this study do not suggest
the presence of a tornado, its occurrence cannot be completely ruled out.
On the predictability of such events, the paper noted the challenges behind
forecasting precise time and location information for localised events more than a
few hours in advance. The paper did note that satellite analysis identified that the
storm developed 3 hours before the accident and kept a coherent trajectory during
its lifetime.
1.12.7 Thunderstorms and downbursts
The Met Office factsheet on thunderstorms32 indicated that they were associated
with convective clouds and are most often, but not necessarily, accompanied
by precipitation at the ground. The factsheet noted the damaging impact of
heavy rainfall, hail, and the electrical discharges associated with thunderstorms.
The factsheet contained limited maritime information and little description of
associated winds.
The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) website mentioned
the risks from strong winds associated with thunderstorms, noting that they can
damage structures and pose risks to aviation33. The UNDRR website described
downbursts as:
powerful, localized columns of sinking air that rapidly descend from
thunderstorms and impact the ground with intense winds, often exceeding
100 km/h34 (54kts).
A combination of evaporative cooling and precipitation drag within the storm
primarily drives these hazardous wind events. Rain or hail evaporates or melts as
it falls through a dry or cooler layer of air below the thunderstorm, cooling the air
and making it denser. This cold dense air plunges rapidly and accelerates. At the
surface the downdraft spreads out radially, generating damaging straight-line winds.
Strong temperature gradients and high atmospheric instability can further intensify
downbursts. While often confused with tornadoes due to their destructive nature,
downbursts produce different wind patterns and are classified as non-rotational.
1.12.8 Guidance for actions in extreme weather
NP45: Admiralty Sailing Directions – Mediterranean Pilot Volume 1
The UK Hydrographic Office (UKHO) published a series of Admiralty Sailing
Directions to provide essential information to support port entry and coastal
navigation. NP45 provided guidance to ships sailing in the western Mediterranean
Sea. Additionally, NP45 contained specific navigational information on Sicily’s
northern coast and off-lying islands.

A section on natural conditions showed typical tracks followed by depressions
in the region. This illustrated that the north Sicilian coast could expect about 19
depressions annually, tracking from the north-west to the south-east.
The guidance indicated that sea surface temperatures usually reached a maximum
in August each year, with associated diagrams showing that the mean sea surface
temperature to the north of Sicily was above 26°C. Similar diagrams showed that
the expected August air pressures north of Sicily would be between 1,014 hPa and

Cold fronts were described as being very active in the region, and they could give
rise to violent conditions with severe squalls and thunderstorms. Thunderstorms
were noted as being at their most frequent in late summer and autumn, although
NP45 did note that the highest frequency occurred in northern and eastern parts of
the area.
Coastal winds were described as being largely controlled by the area’s general
pressure distribution, although straits, headlands and steep-sided valleys may
cause local increases in wind strength due to funnelling. NP45 indicated that the
percentage frequency of force 7 winds in August was less than 2% for the area.
Waterspouts were described as developing when the airflow is very unstable and
relatively frequent in the west and south of the western Mediterranean Sea.
The NP45 data was averaged and referred to specific coastal stations, and
therefore may not be totally representative of the conditions over the open sea or in
approaches to ports in their vicinity.
Climate data for the period from 1974 to 2019 for Punta Raisi, Palermo, Sicily,
located 24.3 miles west-north-west of the accident site, indicated that thunderstorms
occurred on average less than once every August and that gale conditions occurred
on fewer than 0.06% of August days. The mean sea level barometric pressure was
about 1,014 hPa in August.
NP100: Admiralty – The Mariner’s Handbook
The UKHO’s NP100 publication provided general guidance on navigation, sea and
ice conditions, meteorology and regulations. Chapter 5 defined squalls as:
A gust is any sudden, rapid increase of wind of very short duration, typically just
a few seconds… A squall is a sudden increase of mean wind speed which lasts
for several minutes before the wind returns relatively quickly to its previous mean
value. A squall can include many gusts.
On the arrival of a cold front in the northern hemisphere, NP100 stated that any
wind veers markedly to the west or north-west and that this may be accompanied
by sudden squalls. On cyclonic depression in the northern hemisphere, NP100
stated that winds may fall light and variable near the centre of a depression before a
rapid onset of strong or gale-force winds. NP100 did not contain any information on
waterspouts or downbursts.

1.12.9 Low likelihood, high impact weather forecasting
Weather forecasts are predictive in nature and combine scientific understanding of
atmospheric systems with meteorological observations. Marine areas often have a
limited number of observations available to support detailed analysis and description
of specific weather features.
The Met Office described ensemble forecasting as a technique that involves
running a weather prediction model multiple times, each with slightly different
starting conditions35. The set of forecasts generated were known as an ensemble of
member forecasts.
A high degree of confidence could be ascribed to a forecast where there was high
agreement between each member forecast in an ensemble, and less certainty when
agreement between the member forecasts was lower. This technique was employed
in the production of MetArea III forecasts.
The WMO established its Global Multi-Hazard Alert System (GMAS) framework to
support a United Nations initiative to deliver early warning to people of impending
hazard. The GMAS framework included a web-based Severe Weather Information
Centre (SWIC), which collated all authoritative warnings and information related
to extreme and/or potentially high impact weather, water, and climate events
from WMO members36. By early 2024, users could search the SWIC for weather
warnings issued by more than 130 WMO members worldwide.
1.13 REGULATION AND GUIDANCE
1.13.1 Training standards
The MCA set out the UK requirements for the training and certification of deck
officers on large yachts in MSN 1858 (M) Amendment 137. The MSN set out the
implementation of training elements contained in the International Convention on
Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW), 1978,
as amended, and its associated code.
The training programme for the master of a large yacht of less than 500gt was
included in the training programme for yachts up to 3,000gt and contained a
seamanship and meteorology (master yachts) training module. The syllabus
included cloud formation, the local and regional effects of heating and cooling, the
relationship between pressure and wind, and air masses. It also included sections
on tropical storms, and monsoons in the Indian Ocean.
The forecasting element of the syllabus covered the interpretation of marine weather
forecasts, different types of weather messages, organisations providing forecasts,
and the use of forecasts to deduce probable weather conditions and changes. It also
addressed the reliability of forecasts in relation to forecast intervals and duration.
