The meteorology training module did not include thunderstorms, waterspouts,
downbursts, downdrafts or mesocyclonic supercells. Neither did it cover how local
observations may be used to increase forecast accuracy, or the risks that such
weather systems might pose to a sailing vessel.
1.13.2 Large yacht certification scheme
The UK’s large yacht certification scheme began in 1997, with the publication of
LY1. The code provided an alternative regulatory framework based on equivalent
levels of safety to international conventions including the International Convention on
Load Lines, 1966 (ICLL). LY1 was revised and reissued as LY2 in 2004, introducing
updated technical requirements and provisions for short-range yachts. LY2 was
updated to edition 2 on 17 September 2007. A further revision, LY3, came into force
in 2013, incorporating further technical developments and the requirements of the
International Labour Organization’s Maritime Labour Convention, 2006.
The Red Ensign Group (REG) is a partnership of British shipping registries
comprising the UK, Crown Dependencies, and UK Overseas Territories that operate
ship registries38. In 2019, the requirements for the certification of large yachts across
the REG were consolidated into the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code (REG Yacht
Code), creating a unified code for both large commercial yachts and passenger
yachts registered in the REG administrations.
Bayesian was initially surveyed against the requirements of LY2 edition 2. As
the codes were revised and reissued, some elements of the revised codes were
applied retrospectively to existing large yachts. Weathertight integrity and stability
requirements for vessels of Bayesian’s size and type remained unamended when
both LY3 and the REG Yacht Code were introduced.
When Bayesian transitioned to become a pleasure vessel, the requirements set out
in LY2 and any retrospectively applied by LY3 or the REG Yacht Code, as well as the
requirements of the ICLL, ceased to apply.
1.13.3 Pleasure vessel standards
The MCA provided guidance to the operators of pleasure vessels in its MGN 599 (M).
This guidance note directed vessel owners and crew members to the requirements
for the operation of UK registered pleasure vessels. Pleasure vessels of greater than
13.7m in length were defined in the legislation as Class XII vessels. The guidance
included topics subject to regulation including, among others, manning and lifesaving
appliances.
1.13.4 Weathertight integrity
The requirements for the weathertight integrity of large yachts set out in LY2 were
aligned with those of the ICLL. LY2 did allow for arrangements that were considered
to provide an equivalent level of safety and generally required hatches to be kept
closed at sea.

Special consideration was required for windows positioned below the freeboard
deck, noting the need for operational instructions to be provided to the master as to
when strong protective covers should be fitted.
The ventilation of compartments such as the machinery space, which needed to
remain open, also required special consideration, taking into account the effect of
downflooding. Engine exhausts were to be provided with means to prevent back
flooding into the hull through a damaged exhaust system.
1.13.5 Stability requirements
Bayesian was initially assessed against the intact stability standard related to
monohull sailing vessels set out in section 11.2.2.1 of LY2. For compliance with
LY2, statical stability curves were required to be produced for at least the loaded
departure (100% consumables on board) and loaded arrival (10% consumables on
board) conditions.
When outlining these statical stability curves, LY2 required monohull sailing vessels
to have a positive range of stability of not less than 90°, although for vessels of more
than 45m, a range of less than 90° may be considered but may be subject to agreed
operational criteria.
Additionally, a derived heel angle, obtained from the intersection of a derived
wind heeling lever curve and the statical stability curve had to be greater than 15°
(Figure 9). LY2 stated that if the derived heel angle was less than 15° the vessel will
be considered as having insufficient stability for the purpose of the Code.

1.13.6 Liferaft requirements
The arrangement of the stowage, launching and float-free arrangements for the
liferafts on board Bayesian was approved against the requirements of LY2 when it
was built. Liferafts were to be stowed on the weather deck, or in an open space,
and be fitted with HRUs. The HRUs were designed to operate when submerged to
a depth of between 1.5m and 4m so that the liferafts would float free from the vessel
and automatically inflate. The later REG Yacht Code required that:
Liferafts which form part of the float free complement for all vessels regardless
of length or GT shall be capable of floating free, clear of any obstructions with
the vessel in the upright condition.39
Neither LY2 nor the REG Yacht Code considered the float-free capability of liferafts
carried on monohull sailing vessels following a knockdown.
The liferaft stowage arrangements on Bayesian remained unchanged when
the vessel became a pleasure vessel. The arrangements were aligned with the
requirements referenced in MGN 599 (M)40, which required that liferafts be stowed

the liferaft floats free and, if inflatable, inflates automatically when the ship sinks.

1.14 PREVIOUS SIMILAR ACCIDENTS
1.14.1 Island Bay – downflooding, capsize and grounding
On 10 September 2022, the 9.91m passenger vessel Island Bay flooded, capsized
and drifted aground in Carpenter Bay, British Columbia, Canada. The Transportation
Safety Board of Canada (TSB) investigation (TSB report M22P025941) found that the
cumulative effect of modifications to Island Bay had reduced the vessel’s stability
and made it susceptible to heeling, downflooding and capsize. Sustained exposure
to the sea, tidal stream and wind onto the vessel’s side made Island Bay heel
significantly. The combination of environmental effects allowed water to be shipped
on deck, causing the vessel to list. This led to downflooding until the point at which
all reserves of buoyancy were lost and Island Bay capsized.
1.14.2 Concordia – knockdown, capsize and foundering
On 17 February 2010, the 46.5m sail training yacht Concordia was knocked
down, capsized and sank 300nm miles south-south-east of Rio De Janeiro,
Brazil. The 64 crew and trainees on board all managed to abandon ship to the
vessel’s liferafts and were all rescued on 19 February 2010. The TSB investigation
(TSB report M10F000342) found that the vessel had been knocked down in a squall
associated with a likely meteorological downburst, Concordia was also vulnerable
to moderate wind speed increases, and that guidance on the use of squall curves
was not required on many sail training vessels. Additionally, training in the use of
squall curves was not required for crew certification in sail training vessels. The
investigation also found that the risk of knockdown, despite being well known,
had not resulted in their consequences being prepared for: three of eight liferafts
became inaccessible, a further liferaft was damaged following deployment and
the remaining four liferafts were difficult to release. The report further identified
that, despite indications of the impending weather, the officer of the watch did not
perceive any threat to the vessel.
The TSB issued Marine Safety Advisory Letter 06/10: Considerations and
Precautions Regarding Knockdown of Sailing Vessels highlighting the risks
of knockdowns in sail training vessels, and advised operators to review their
procedures when in squalls. The TSB also recommended that initiatives be
undertaken to adopt international standards on the provision of stability guidance to
assist officers assessing the risk of knockdown and capsize.
1.14.3 Pride of Baltimore – knockdown, capsize and foundering
On 14 May 1986, the 27.4m sailing vessel Pride of Baltimore was knocked down,
capsized and foundered with the loss of four lives about 250nm north of Puerto
Rico in the Caribbean Sea. The USA National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB)
investigation (NTSB report PB87-91640143) found that the Pride of Baltimore had
been knocked down to port after a sudden thunderstorm downburst of high velocity
winds that exceeded the limits of the vessel’s stability. Following the knockdown
there was extensive downflooding due to the lack of watertight bulkheads in the hull.

Liferafts were challenging to access as they were stowed under the tiller and had to
be released by hand. One liferaft was eventually orally inflated and eight of the 12

The vessel’s crew were unaware of the impending hazard because they had no
forecast for the high winds, or any warnings of the potential for these to develop near
thunderstorms. The NTSB made a recommendation to the US National Weather
Service to include in its Marine High Seas forecasts a warning of the potential
for rapidly developing high winds near thunderstorms. This recommendation was
particular to situations where no specific knowledge of thunderstorm intensity
was available.

SECTION 2 – ANALYSIS
2.1 AIM
The purpose of the analysis is to determine the contributory causes and
circumstances of the accident as a basis for making recommendations to prevent
similar accidents occurring in the future.
2.2 OVERVIEW
Bayesian was knocked down by extreme winds that were not explicitly forecast.
Bayesian did not recover, downflooded and sank. No liferafts were released
automatically. The crew released one liferaft manually and it was boarded by 15
survivors before their rescue. One crew member and six passengers drowned.
This section of the report examines the factors that contributed to the foundering
of Bayesian, including the yacht’s stability and the effects of high wind on its
ability to remain upright with no sails set; the weather information available; crew
preparations; and the provision of lifesaving equipment.
2.3 THE ACCIDENT
Bayesian was anchored close to the breakwater at Porticello before it foundered.
The weather forecasts received during the day before the accident had identified
the possibility of thunderstorms in the general area around Porticello, but did not
explicitly warn of the risk of accompanying winds. Bayesian’s master recognised
the possibility of strong winds and had left instructions to be woken by the overnight
watchkeepers if the wind speed rose or the yacht started dragging the anchor.
The winds were light and the seas calm when Bayesian’s crew and guests retired
for the night, and they were unaware of the possibility of significant weather of the
magnitude experienced passing through the anchorage. The local weather remained
benign until about 11 minutes before the knockdown.
The master and off-duty crew were woken up when the wind increased beyond the
limit set by the master in their night orders and Bayesian began to drag its anchor.
Having had recent experience of dragging anchor in strong winds, the master and
crew did not perceive any immediate danger from the yacht’s movement. Some of
the crew started to prepare the main engines to enable the master to manoeuvre
Bayesian while others started to secure loose items of equipment and mitigate the
effects of the wind and the heavy rain.
The shore was approximately 5nm away to the south-south-east in the direction
Bayesian was travelling. The need for urgent action to manoeuvre the yacht away
from a possible grounding was not immediate.
None of the crew on board Bayesian were aware of a risk of knockdown in high
winds when the sails were not raised. They did not therefore perceive an immediate
need to close and secure all external hull doors and flush hatches to improve its
weathertight integrity to account for such a risk.
40
As the wind increased and Bayesian heeled over to starboard at an estimated angle
of between 10° and 20°, the yacht reached an angle similar to that experienced
while under sail. The downflooding points on board were not immersed at this angle
of heel. The crew’s continued perception was that dragging the anchor and weather
damage to items of upper deck furniture were the only risks to be managed.
The crew were unaware of the critical knockdown hazard and were focused on
minimising anchor drag and securing the yacht. By attempting to use the engines to
point Bayesian into the wind, the master was inadvertently also acting to reduce the
risk of knockdown; however, there was insufficient time to complete the manoeuvre.
The postmortem reports indicated the presence of alcohol in all of the deceased.
Recognising the possibility that at least a proportion of the alcohol found was
generated after death, the levels detected are not considered to have influenced the
outcome of the accident.
Six passengers and one crew member died when Bayesian was knocked down
by an extreme wind that heeled it over to an angle from which it could not recover.
Flooding into the internal spaces of the vessel caused it to founder approximately
18 minutes later.
2.4 VESSEL STABILITY
2.4.1 Vulnerability in the motoring condition
The initial study conducted by the Wolfson Unit compared the stability model used
by the MCA for the original approval of the SIB with the yacht as examined after the
accident. While the stability model used by the MCA had simplified some aspects,
the effect was not significant and the Wolfson Unit study concluded that the SIB
reflected the stability of the yacht to an acceptable degree.
The SIB included curves of maximum steady heel angle to prevent downflooding in
gusts for various sailing conditions. The Wolfson Unit studies showed that the mast
and furled sails contributed significantly to the heeling moment applied to the vessel
by wind but the SIB did not include any information on its effect in the motoring
condition with the centreboard raised and no sails set. The crew on board were
therefore unaware of the risk that high winds posed to Bayesian in this configuration.
Similar to the accident involving Concordia in 2010, without knowledge of the
vulnerability of Bayesian to extreme weather, no actions to mitigate the risk of
knockdown in the motoring condition had been identified and included in the SIB for
the guidance of the crew.
The vulnerability of Bayesian to wind heeling moments while in the motoring
condition had never been assessed, resulting in the crew being unaware of a critical
risk to the vessel and unable to take account of it in their operations.
2.4.2 Knockdown risk
Knockdown was a recognised hazard for a vessel under sail. Bayesian’s master was
aware that this risk extended to large yachts, having previously experienced one.
That vessel had recovered successfully.
41
When under sail, Bayesian had an identified angle of vanishing stability of less
than the 90° stipulated in LY2 that the SIB had been originally approved against.
The reduced angle of vanishing stability was identified when the vessel was in the
light load sailing condition with the centreboard lowered. To use the relaxation of
this requirement provided for larger yachts in LY2, Bayesian was fitted with a sail
control system that would automatically shed load from the sails to minimise the
knockdown risk.
Independent of the sail monitoring and control system, the crew were able to reef,
furl or drop the sails when sailing to further mitigate any risk of knockdown. Such
mitigations did not apply to the motoring condition with no sails up and, in any case,
the vessel’s vulnerability to knockdown in this condition was unknown because it
had not been assessed.
The Wolfson Unit study commissioned by the MAIB indicated that, in the conditions
assessed, Bayesian was vulnerable to extreme winds on the beam. Further, that
any knockdown in this condition would be irrecoverable once the yacht passed the
angle of vanishing stability, assessed in the probable loss condition as being 73°.
Regardless of the wind velocity, once Bayesian had passed this angle of heel it
could not right itself.
The derived wind heeling data in the Wolfson Unit study for the probable loss
condition identified that when the yacht was initially heeled to between 10° and
20° it was at an angle where a risk of knockdown from a significant gust of wind
likely existed.
It was not possible to determine the effect of the movement of items on board
Bayesian as the heel increased. The movement of liquids, stores and other items
would have increased the heeling moment, reducing the ability of the vessel to
resist capsize.
The winds experienced were almost certainly of sufficient magnitude and duration
to cause a heeling moment that resulted in Bayesian heeling beyond its angle of
vanishing stability, an angle from which it could not recover.
2.4.3 Stability information booklet guidance
Bayesian’s SIB provided generic guidance to the master on the prevention of
capsize. This guidance did not define what might be considered adverse weather
or a severe squall or when specific interventions would be required. Only the
instruction to keep the door from the engine room to the lazarette closed when the
port side shell door was open related to the yacht being at anchor. On the night of
the accident that shell door was shut.
The SIB listed actions to be taken by the crew to prepare for a rough weather
passage. However, Bayesian was not intending to depart on passage through heavy
weather at the time of the accident so such activities were neither planned nor
initiated before the yacht was knocked down.
Other than providing a generic instruction to close the openings on board Bayesian
before departing in heavy weather, the SIB did not set out any need to do so at
anchor. Similarly, it did not provide guidance on how to manoeuvre the yacht to
account for such weather.
42
When in the lowered position, the centreboard lowered Bayesian’s centre of
gravity and therefore increased the yacht’s righting moment. However, the SIB only
indicated that the centreboard needed to be in this position in the sailing conditions
it contained.
Lowering of Bayesian’s centreboard while at anchor increased the yacht’s propensity
to yaw, increasing the likelihood of it dragging its anchor. With no guidance in the
SIB, or elsewhere, about use of the centreboard at anchor, it was not the practice
to have it lowered. This reduced the risk of dragging the anchor, a risk that the
crew were aware of, but inadvertently increased the vulnerability of Bayesian to
knockdown in high winds; a risk that the crew were unaware of.
Bayesian’s SIB contained generic instructions on when or why precautions for
watertight integrity and downflooding should be applied. This limited its usefulness
in supporting the crew’s preparations for an approaching storm when the yacht was
at anchor.
2.4.4 Downflooding
Bayesian’s crew were unaware of the risk of knockdown when in the motoring
condition and the SIB did not define under what circumstances the listed generic
precautions against downflooding should be applied. The crew’s actions in the
lead-up to the accident were therefore in response to the heavy rain and dragging
of the anchor and not specifically to mitigate any risk of downflooding in the event
of excessive heel. With no perceived need, some external doors, flush hatches and
hull openings remained unsecured.
Bayesian initially heeled over to an angle estimated to be between 10° and 20° to
starboard. At this angle none of the openings that would allow water to enter the hull
were immersed, and no downflooding occurred.
At the point of knockdown, Bayesian took less than 15 seconds to go from the
previous 10° to 20° of heel to lying flat in the water. During this period, downflooding
would start, allowing water to enter through the yacht’s openings.
In the light load motoring condition set out in the SIB, critical flooding would begin
when the angle of heel passed through 47.5° with progressive flooding into other
spaces as the angle of heel increased further. Water would also enter over the sides
of the yacht.
Bayesian was knocked down in a very short period of time. It is therefore unlikely
that the volume of water entering the vessel during the period between the
downflooding points being first immersed and the yacht lying on its side had any
material effect on the knockdown. Once past the angle of vanishing stability,
Bayesian was unable to right itself.
When Bayesian was lying on its side, the open accesses near the centreline
leading to the guest and crew accommodation spaces would also have been
at least partially submerged. Similar to the accidents involving Concordia and
Pride of Baltimore, once knocked down, water was able to freely flow into the
below-deck compartments.
43
It was not possible to determine whether the sinking would have been prevented or
slowed significantly had all openings been shut and secured. The state of openings
had negligible impact of the knockdown and only become relevant once Bayesian
was on its side and capsizing.
The effect of the very heavy rainfall Bayesian experienced was considered in the
second Wolfson Unit study. It was determined that the influence of rain accumulating
between decks was not a significant factor in the time Bayesian was exposed to it.
It is unlikely that downflooding into Bayesian’s internal spaces had a material effect
on its foundering until the yacht was lying on its side, by which time it was unable to
right itself.
2.4.5 Red Ensign Group Yacht Code requirements
Bayesian was a monohull sailing vessel built to the requirements of LY2. Although
not required, it was maintained substantially to the standards of that code and the
applicable requirements of the REG Yacht Code.
LY2 allowed Bayesian to have an angle of vanishing stability of less than 90° and
the agreed operational criteria required by LY2 was contained in the approved SIB.
The agreed operational criteria related to the automatic sail monitoring and control
system and its ability to shed the wind heeling load with the yacht under sail.
Wind heeling levers were a factor in the accidents involving both Concordia and
Pride of Baltimore. Both LY2 and the later REG Yacht Code required curves of
statical stability and wind heeling limits to be provided, but only for vessels when
in the sailing condition. However, like the accident involving Island Bay, high winds
had the ability to generate significant heeling moments for Bayesian while in the
motoring condition with sails down.
The Wolfson Unit study concluded that Bayesian, in its probable loss condition,
similar to the motoring condition with sails down and the centreboard in the raised
position, was vulnerable to winds on the beam. It further concluded that the steady
state wind heeling limit and the angle of vanishing stability in this condition were
lower than when in the sailing condition.
Neither LY2 nor the later REG Yacht Code required the assessment of the
vulnerability of monohull sailing yachts with an angle of vanishing stability below 90°
to high winds when operating without sails set, placing the people on such vessels
at an undetermined risk.
2.4.6 Approval of minimum downflooding angle
The list of openings and their associated downflooding angles contained in the SIB
indicated that there were openings on Bayesian that became immersed at an angle
of heel of less than 40°.
The LY2 requirement for minimum downflooding angle stated that No opening
regardless of size which may lead to progressive flooding should be immersed at
an angle of heel of less than 40°. It did not reference the greater critical flooding
44
angle that was a calculated value based on the area of the openings progressively
immersed with increasing angle of heel. The approved SIB did not comment on how
these openings were treated against the LY2 requirement.
At the time that the SIB was approved, Bayesian did not meet the LY2 requirements
for minimum downflooding angle and was therefore vulnerable to progressive
flooding at angles below that required by the code.
2.5 WEATHER AND CLIMATE INFORMATION
2.5.1 Weather forecasts
Prior warning of low probability, high impact events is a significant challenge to all
weather forecasters. The official forecasts of Météo-France and CNMCA for the
night of the accident predicted sustained winds of up to force 5, with gusts of up
to 40% stronger, across the Lipari sea area and Tyrrhenian Sea coastal regions.
Having specifically mentioned thunderstorms, these official forecasts further
described associated strong wind gusts but did not detail their strength or severity.
High observed values for CAPE and elevated sea surface temperatures both
meant that there was significant energy feeding the weather system. The resulting
instability meant that damaging winds were possible along the north coast of Sicily.
The forecasts did not account for features and no associated warnings for violent
winds or downbursts were issued. Other than this specific risk, the official forecasts
did reflect the predominant weather experienced across the wider sea areas and
coastal regions in question.
From the time Bayesian’s master went to bed on 18 August 2024 until the time of
the accident, there were no weather forecasts that explicitly warned of the risk of
downbursts with damaging hurricane force winds.
The master had recognised the possibility of high winds, leaving instructions to be
woken by the overnight watchkeepers should this rise above a set limit. However,
similar to the findings of the investigation into the knockdown and foundering
of Pride of Baltimore, the official weather forecasts did not forewarn the crew
of Bayesian to the risk of extreme weather and of the possibility of hurricane
force winds.
The official weather forecasts for the area of the accident, although broadly
accurate, did not communicate the potential severity and impact of the predicted
thunderstorms, limiting the crew’s ability to recognise the developing hazard and
take timely action.
2.5.2 The weather experienced
It is not possible to determine the exact weather phenomenon that generated the
extreme winds experienced in the anchorage off Porticello on 19 August 2024.
Reported sightings of a feature resembling a waterspout could not be discounted.
However, all of the possible weather events analysed contained the potential to
generate extreme wind speeds.
45
The very localised winds experienced made both Sir Robert Baden Powell and
Bayesian drag their anchors in a near-straight line, making it most likely that the
winds persisted in the same direction during the period while the vessels were
dragging. As waterspouts do not feature straight-line winds, they were unlikely to
have been the driving weather phenomenon during the accident.
The extreme winds experienced by Bayesian were most likely the result of a
downburst associated with a convective windstorm.
2.5.3 Guidance on weather features
Mobile depressions, thunderstorms and waterspouts were described in NP45’s
general information on weather features that may be encountered in the
Mediterranean Sea.
The general meteorological guidance provided in NP100 included specific
information related to tropical storms and using local observations to determine how
forecast weather might be experienced locally. However, it did not contain reference
to thunderstorms, waterspouts, downbursts, downdrafts or mesocyclonic supercells,
or how these features might change with local effects and features.
On board Bayesian, and in all the previous similar accidents identified, the impact of
the local environment was significantly underappreciated by those facing the effects
of the weather at the time.
The guidance provided in the UKHO’s Admiralty publications provided insufficient
information for thunderstorms, waterspouts, downbursts, downdrafts or
mesocyclonic supercells to help mariners prepare for the risks they present.
2.5.4 Training requirements for meteorology
The required knowledge of seamanship and meteorology for the issue of a UK
certificate of competency for masters serving on large yachts was contained in
MSN 1858 (M) Amendment 1. The holder of a UK certificate of competence was not
required to understand the factors that could contribute to the generation of squalls
and violent wind gusts. The report into the loss of Concordia identified a lack of
knowledge of squall curves on sailing vessels as being contributory to that accident.
Local effects can modify the predominant weather experienced more broadly
across a larger geographic area. With mountains nearby, elevated sea surface
temperatures and forecast thunderstorms, there was much to indicate that
such local effects could impact the weather in the anchorage off Porticello. The
significance of all these weather features was not detailed in official guidance or
training, limiting the ability of Bayesian’s crew to interpret their observations and the
information available to assess the level of risk present.
The UK training syllabus for masters of large sailing vessels did not provide
sufficient information to support the assessment of risk when proximate to
severe thunderstorms.
46
2.6 ESCAPE AND LIFESAVING
2.6.1 Accommodation escape routes
Guests G1 and G2 were already awake when Bayesian was knocked down and
escaped from their cabin on the lower deck, exiting via the main guest stairwell into
the saloon. They were the only people to escape from the guest cabin area once
Bayesian was lying on its side.
The investigation did not have access to dive records identifying the precise
locations of the casualties and debris within the wreck. These records might have
assisted in determining their movements following the knockdown. It is therefore
unknown why the other guests in the accommodation areas were unable to escape.
The remaining people in the guest cabin area, and any loose items, would have
fallen to the starboard side when Bayesian was knocked down. For those in cabins
on the yacht’s starboard side, it is likely that they were either thrown into a position
from where they were unable to ascend to reach the exit from their cabins or
lacked the physical ability to do so. For those on the port side, it is possible that
falling debris may have blocked the inward opening doors. Any delay increased the
likelihood that the incoming water would prevent their escape.
The chef was last seen in the galley, and it is most likely that he was in this
compartment when the knockdown happened. The chef would have been subject to
the same issues as those in the cabin area; falling to the starboard side of the space
along with any loose items and having to ascend to escape the compartment.
Though the chef probably sustained his injuries during knockdown, given he was
located outside the wreck, it is almost certain that he did manage to escape the hull
following the knockdown. The investigation was unable to establish what route he
took to escape or whether he left doors or hatches open behind him.
The rapid knockdown of Bayesian limited the time available to escape from the
lower deck. Occupants were hindered by altered orientation, potential obstructions
and rapidly worsening flooding conditions, which significantly reduced their ability to
escape the yacht before it sank.
2.6.2 Abandon ship
The accident to Bayesian developed within a short period of time; from apparently
benign conditions at 0352, to dragging anchor at around 0357, then to being
knocked down in hurricane force winds at 0406.
In the early stages of the accident there was no perceived need to alert the
guests. The speed and distance that both Bayesian and Sir Robert Baden
Powell were dragging their anchors gave no immediate concern that the vessels
would run aground or require the mustering of the guests on board either vessel.
When Bayesian was knocked down, all those on board reacted to the situation
they found themselves in, and any attempt to initiate the emergency procedures
became superfluous.
47
During the abandonment of Bayesian, the crew needed to respond to a rapidly
developing situation that had not been anticipated in the on board drills. The master
was able to direct the abandonment, overseeing the evacuation of the guests and
crew in the upper areas of the vessel, and instructing survivors to enter the water
and swim clear.
Crew members took independent action where necessary, including the release of
the EPIRB to transmit a distress alert and the delivery of first aid to the injured.
The manual release of the liferaft from Bayesian provided the means for those
crew and guests able to escape from the vessel to survive while awaiting rescue.
Bayesian’s crew were familiar with the equipment inside the liferaft, and this enabled
them to signal for assistance and care for the people on board.
The emergency procedures and drills undertaken on board Bayesian did not
anticipate a casualty of a type or pace that effectively bypassed the formal muster
and evacuation arrangements.
The safety of those crew and guests able to leave Bayesian following the accident
relied heavily on the training, experience and initiative of individual crew members.
2.6.3 Liferaft release
None of the liferafts on Bayesian were released automatically from the yacht when it
foundered, requiring the crew to manually release the port side forward liferaft.
When Bayesian was initially knocked down, the liferafts on the starboard side were
inaccessible and it was not possible to determine whether the HRUs had activated
at that time. At the point of knockdown, the HRUs for the port side liferafts were
unlikely to have submerged sufficiently for the hydrostatic pressure to activate them.
After the accident, all of the HRUs were found to have operated and the buoyant
liferafts were held in place by the stowage arrangement. Two of the three liferafts
that remained on board when Bayesian sank were released from the wreck during
the salvage operation. Both liferafts operated as designed on release, inflating and
separating from the vessel.
The liferaft stowage arrangements on Bayesian met the regulatory requirements
to which they were initially surveyed. LY2 required liferafts to release, float free
and inflate but did not specifically require consideration of their ability to do so
after a knockdown. Later regulation in the REG Yacht Code required only that
liferafts be capable of floating free, clear of any obstructions with the vessel in the
upright condition.
Regulatory requirements for the float-free arrangements for liferafts did not
adequately account for the knockdown and sinking scenario applicable to large
sailing yachts.
48
SECTION 3 – CONCLUSIONS
3.1 SAFETY ISSUES DIRECTLY CONTRIBUTING TO THE
ACCIDENT THAT HAVE BEEN ADDRESSED OR RESULTED IN
RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Six passengers and one crew member died when Bayesian was knocked down
by an extreme wind that heeled it over to an angle from which it could not recover.
Flooding into the internal spaces of the vessel caused it to founder approximately
18 minutes later. [2.3]
2. The vulnerability of Bayesian to wind heeling moments while in the motoring
condition had never been assessed, resulting in the crew being unaware of a critical
risk to the vessel and unable to take account of it in their operations. [2.4.1]
3. The extreme winds experienced were almost certainly of sufficient magnitude and
duration to cause a heeling moment that resulted in Bayesian heeling beyond its
angle of vanishing stability, an angle from which it could not recover. [2.4.2]
4. Bayesian’s SIB contained generic instructions on when or why precautions for
watertight integrity and downflooding should be applied. This limited its usefulness in
supporting the crew’s preparations for an approaching storm when the yacht was at
anchor. [2.4.3]
5. It is unlikely that downflooding into Bayesian’s internal spaces had a material effect
on its foundering until the yacht was lying on its side, by which time it was unable to
right itself. [2.4.4]
6. Neither LY2 nor the later REG Yacht Code required the assessment of the
vulnerability of monohull sailing yachts with an angle of vanishing stability below 90°
to high winds when operating without sails set, placing the people on such vessels
at an undetermined risk. [2.4.5]
7. The official weather forecasts for the area of the accident, although broadly
accurate, did not communicate the potential severity and impact of the predicted
thunderstorms, limiting the crew’s ability to recognise the developing hazard and
take timely action. [2.5.1]
8. The extreme winds experienced by Bayesian were most likely the result of a
downburst associated with a convective windstorm. [2.5.2]
9. The guidance provided in the UKHO’s Admiralty publications provided insufficient
information for thunderstorms, waterspouts, downbursts, downdrafts or
mesocyclonic supercells to help mariners to prepare for the risks they present.
[2.5.3]
10. The UK training syllabus for masters of large sailing vessels did not provide
sufficient information to support the assessment of risk when proximate to severe
thunderstorms. [2.5.4]
49
3.2 SAFETY ISSUES NOT DIRECTLY CONTRIBUTING TO THE
ACCIDENT THAT HAVE BEEN ADDRESSED OR RESULTED IN
RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Regulatory requirements for the float-free arrangements of liferafts did not
adequately account for the knockdown and sinking scenario applicable to large
sailing yachts. [2.6.3]
3.3 OTHER SAFETY ISSUES NOT DIRECTLY CONTRIBUTING TO THE
ACCIDENT
1. At the time that the SIB was approved, Bayesian did not meet the LY2 requirements
for minimum downflooding angle and was therefore vulnerable to progressive
flooding at angles below that required by the code. [2.4.6]
2. The rapid knockdown of Bayesian limited the time available to escape from the
lower deck. Occupants were hindered by altered orientation, potential obstructions
and rapidly worsening flooding conditions, which significantly reduced their ability to
escape the yacht before it sank. [2.6.1]
3.4 SAFETY LEARNING
1. The safety of those crew and guests able to leave Bayesian following the accident
relied heavily on the training, experience and initiative of individual crew members.
[2.6.2]
50
SECTION 4 – ACTIONS TAKEN
4.1 MAIB ACTIONS
The MAIB has:
● Issued an interim report into the accident (Annex C).
● Issued a safety flyer to the yachting industry (Annex D).
● Prepared a paper detailing the hazards identified in this report, for consideration
by the casualty analysis group, to be submitted to the 13th session of the IMO
Sub-Committee on Implementation of IMO Instruments (III).
4.2 ACTIONS TAKEN BY OTHER ORGANISATIONS
No safety actions have been taken by other organisations.
51
SECTION 5 – RECOMMENDATIONS
The Red Ensign Group is recommended to:
2026/162 Complete a study of the vulnerability of monohull sailing vessels that are
certified under the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code to the risk of knockdown
with no sails set.
2026/163 Amend the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code as appropriate to the study’s
findings and publish guidance on identified vulnerabilities.
2026/164 Amend guidance on the content of the stability information booklet carried
on board vessels certified to the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code with respect
to preparations to be taken in advance of forecast extreme weather, whether
underway or at anchor.
2026/165 Amend the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code to ensure that liferafts installed on
all sailing vessels vulnerable to knockdown are stowed to permit them to float
free from their stowage, inflate, and break free from the vessel in the event of
its sinking.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is recommended to:
2026/166 Review and, where appropriate, amend yacht officer seamanship and
meteorology syllabi to ensure candidates can recognise severe convective
weather hazards including thunderstorms, downbursts and extreme wind
gusts to assist in the application of appropriate precautions when sailing,
motoring or at anchor.
The Met Office is recommended to:
2026/167 Invite the World Meteorological Organization Worldwide Met-Ocean
Information and Warning Service Sub-Committee to consider how low
likelihood, high-impact weather hazards should be represented within future
data services.
The UK Hydrographic Office is recommended to:
2026/168 Liaise with the Met Office and Maritime and Coastguard Agency to develop
and update guidance on the risks of extreme weather events for inclusion
in NP45: Admiralty Sailing Directions – Mediterranean Pilot Volume 1 and
NP100: Admiralty – The Mariner’s Handbook as appropriate.
Safety recommendations shall in no case create a presumption of blame or liability
52

Summary
At 1851 (
UTC
+1) on 28 October 2013, the
RoPax
ferry Stena Alegra grounded after dragging its anchor in 76 knot winds off Karlskrona, Sweden.
The vessel’s bottom plating and frames were damaged, and one ballast tank and one void space were flooded. Two tugs towed the vessel off the rocks after the weather had moderated the next day. Following an underwater inspection the vessel proceeded to Gdynia, Poland, for repair.
Safety lessons
the master had decided to anchor the vessel in winds that were forecast to increase to the assumed maximum design limit of its anchoring equipment without completing a full assessment of the consequent risks
the wind speed rose to above that forecast, causing the vessel to drag its anchor. Measures aimed at arresting the vessel’s drift failed to prevent Stena Alegra from running aground
Recommendations
Recommendations have been made to the vessel’s manager, Northern Marine Management Ltd, to enhance its safety management system requirements for anchoring, including contingency planning, and the enhancement of masters’ handover procedures.

The wind speed rose to above that forecast, causing the vessel to drag its anchor. Measures aimed at
arresting the vessel’s drift failed to prevent Stena Alegra from running aground.
Recommendations have been made to the vessel’s manager, Northern Marine Management Ltd, to
enhance its safety management system requirements for anchoring, including contingency planning, and
the enhancement of masters’ handover procedures.
FACTUAL INFORMATION
Vessel
On 27 May 2013, while laid up in Falmouth, UK, Stena Alegra was purchased by Stena North Sea Ltd.
The vessel was then towed to Gdansk, Poland, for a major refit under the management of Northern
Marine Management Ltd (NMM).
On 8 July 2013 the vessel was chartered to Stena Line and entered service between Gdynia and
Karlskrona. An ‘Operational Limits’ certificate, issued by the UK’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency on
19 September 2013, included a ‘Sea State Restriction’ of 4 metres significant wave height. In accordance
with Merchant Shipping Notice (MSN) 1790 (M), this allowed Stena Alegra to operate the route between
Gdynia and Karlskrona for which a significant wave height of 2.9 metres had been determined.
Stena Alegra was one of three vessels on the service and was scheduled to sail from Gdynia on
Wednesday, Friday and Sunday, and from Karlskrona on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. The schedule
included overnight layovers in Gdynia on Saturday night, and Karlskrona on Monday night.
Environment
When Stena Alegra dragged its anchor the weather conditions in the area were south-westerly winds
gusting 76 knots (Beaufort Force 12), a moderate sea state, and good visibility.
NARRATIVE
At 1800 on Sunday 27 October 2013, Stena Alegra sailed from Gdynia for its overnight crossing to
Karlskrona. Once clear of the port the master handed over the watch to the third officer and left the
bridge. He went to sleep in his cabin at about 2200. At 0400 he was called by the OOW3 because a
passenger had suffered a stroke, and went to the bridge. In an effort to expedite the vessel’s arrival at
Karlskrona the master agreed with the pilot, by VHF4 radio, that the pilot could board the vessel once it
was north of the submarine nets between Aspo and Tjurkö (Figure 2) rather than at the usual boarding
position. The master then took the con, with the second officer remaining on the bridge to support
the master until relieved by the chief officer. At 0550, the pilot boarded, followed shortly afterwards by
paramedics to assist the sick passenger.
Stena Alegra was berthed by the master using one of the two bow thrusters, owing to a fault with one
of its two diesel generators. Wind conditions at the time were approximately south-west 28 knots. After
making fast, three of the four main engines were stopped while the cargo was discharged. No 3 main
engine was left running to power a shaft alternator while the faulty diesel generator was under repair.
During the short time alongside, the master discussed with the pilot his intention to proceed to anchor in
anchorage B (Figure 2) for the vessel’s scheduled layover period. The master proposed anchoring as
close to the main channel as possible to gain maximum sea room from Aspeskarsklapparna, owing to
the forecast south-westerly winds. During these discussions, the pilot produced a local weather forecast

that indicated winds would increase in excess of 40 knots and peak at about 2100 that evening. The pilot
also commented that anchoring Stena Alegra south-west of its normal anchoring position should provide
better holding ground because the seabed would be less disturbed. The local weather forecast predicted
wind speeds similar to the vessel’s NAVTEX5 forecast of 18-24 metres/second (35-47 knots).
At 0800, after completing cargo discharge, Stena Alegra departed its berth for the anchorage. The wind
had increased to 30 knots. The master had the con with the pilot providing advice. At 0827, the master
ordered the starboard anchor to be let go. By 0845, Stena Alegra was ‘brought up’6 with 8 shackles7
of anchor cable having been deployed. The vessel’s bridge was positioned with Godnatt bearing
approximately 267°(T)8 at 0.82 mile.
The master then discussed the availability of the main engines with the chief engineer, and requested
that they remain on 5 minutes’ notice throughout the vessel’s time at anchor. The chief engineer wanted
to keep a shaft alternator running while the faulty diesel generator was under repair. He therefore
suggested that No 3 main engine be kept running and available to be clutched in immediately should
it be required, with the other engines to be started as quickly as possible afterwards. Following this
conversation, No 1, 2 and 4 main engines were shut down and No 3 main engine remained running with
the shaft alternator engaged to supply electrical power.
The master then handed over the anchor watch to the third officer, and left written instructions for the
OOW to instruct the engine room to clutch in the main engine that was running and to call both him and
the bosun should he suspect that the vessel was dragging its anchor. These instructions also advised the
OOW that the wind was due to increase to over 40 knots.
At 1200, the third officer handed over the watch to the second officer on the bridge and the fourth
engineer handed over the watch to the third engineer in the engine room. Both outgoing officers verbally
passed on to their reliefs the master’s requirement for the main engines to remain at 5 minutes’ notice. At
that time the wind remained blowing from the south-west at about 30 knots.
By 1300, the wind had increased and the master had started visiting the bridge about every 15 minutes
to check on the wind speed; he was also monitoring the forecast conditions via the internet.
By about 1600, the wind speed had increased to 40 knots. Stena Alegra was maintaining its anchored
position, but had started to yaw9 by up to 60º either side of the wind direction. At 1646, a NAVTEX
forecast was received predicting south-westerly winds at 18-25 metres/second (36 to 50 knots).
By 1700, the wind speed had increased to 50 knots and the repair to the faulty diesel generator had been
completed. The chief engineer informed the master, who decided that No 3 main engine should remain
running and ready to be clutched in immediately should it be required.
At 1800, the watches changed; the third officer took over on the bridge, and the fourth engineer took over
in the engine room. At the time of the handover, the wind speed was around 53 knots. The master was
also on the bridge and had observed the wind speed on the anemometer. Hoping that the wind strength
had reached its peak, he went to have dinner with the chief officer.
5 NAVTEX (Navigational Telex) is an international automated medium frequency direct-printing service for delivery of
navigational and meteorological warnings and forecasts, as well as urgent marine safety information to ships.
6 A vessel is said to be ‘brought up’ when all way has stopped, it is riding to its anchor, and the anchor is holding.
7 A shackle of anchor cable measures 27.5 metres.
8 True
9 The sideways movement and rotation around the vertical axis of a vessel at anchor.
4
At 1830, the master and chief officer returned to the bridge, noting a wind speed of about 51 knots on
their arrival. The chief officer went to the chart room at the back of the bridge and began preparing a
loading programme for the next day, while the master returned to his cabin. Approximately 10 minutes
later, the chief officer became concerned by ‘strange noises’ coming from the focsle10. Fearing that the
starboard anchor windlass brake might not be holding, the chief officer returned to the front of the bridge
and visually monitored the focsle. He then told the third officer that he would take one of the duty ABs11
with him to inspect the anchor cable.
Before the chief officer left the bridge, the master returned and noted that the anemometer was
registering a wind speed of 66 knots. At approximately 1847, the master looked at the ECS12 display
and saw the vessel’s history trail, which had been scribing a consistent arc over the last few hours, start
to move astern. He immediately instructed the third officer to call the engine control room to “start the
second engine quickly and clutch in the first”. The third officer used the internal telephone system to
call the engine control room and pass on the master’s orders, which were acknowledged by the fourth
engineer. The fourth engineer slowed down No 3 main engine in preparation to engage the clutch, and
then began to start the other main engines.
At 1848, the master sent the third officer to the chief engineer’s cabin to ask for No 3 main engine to be
clutched in. On receiving the master’s request, the chief engineer told the third officer to call the engine
control room and pass the message to the duty engineer. He then proceeded to the engine control room
himself.
The third officer returned to the bridge and, at 1849, a second call was made to the engine control room
stating “we need to start right now”. This call was again answered by the fourth engineer. Stena Alegra
continued to drag its anchor and drift north-eastwards at about 3 knots.
At 1851, Stena Alegra’s forepart grounded on rocks adjacent to Aspeskarsklapparna. Approximately 20
seconds later, the control of all four main engines and two bow thrusters were handed over to the bridge.
The master attempted to manoeuvre the vessel clear of the rocks by splitting the engines13 and using the
bow thrusters and rudders. During this time he instructed the duty AB to call the crew, alerted the pilot
station and coastguard by VHF radio, informed NMM by mobile telephone, and gave instructions for the
tanks and void spaces to be sounded.
At 1905, the master stopped his attempts to free the vessel and left the engines running with zero
propeller pitch applied. No 17 void space was found to be flooded.
At 2135, the tug Dutch Power, which had been moored in Karlskrona, arrived on scene to assist, and was
made fast to Stena Alegra’s stern. Stena Alegra remained aground overnight.
During the morning of 29 October 2013, officials from the Swedish coastguard arrived with a
classification society surveyor and divers to carry out a damage inspection. At 1000, No 6 ballast tank
was found to be flooded. At approximately 1655, with moderating weather conditions and a second tug
assisting, Stena Alegra was pulled off the rocks and re-anchored in anchorage B.
10 Forecastle – forward mooring station, where the anchor windlass and mooring winches are located
11 Able seaman – a deck rating
12 Electronic Chart System
13 To place port and starboard propeller pitch controls in opposite directions, ie one side ahead and one side astern to generate
a turning moment at the vessel’s stern.
5
Manning and watchkeeping
The master was Romanian and 51 years old. He was on his first contract with NMM and had joined
Stena Alegra on 16 October 2013 for a familiarisation and handover period with the offgoing master. He
formally took command of Stena Alegra on 27 October 2013 in Gdynia. Prior to joining NMM he had
served as master predominantly on Ro-Ro14 vessels and had gained some RoPax experience since
2002. He had obtained a Romanian STCW15 II/2 Master Unlimited Certificate of Competency in 1996.
The third officer was Polish and 39 years old. He had worked for NMM for about 2 years and had joined
Stena Alegra on 25 September 2013 for his second contract on board. He had held a Polish STCW II/1
OOW Unlimited Certificate since 2001, and had gained about 6 years’ experience as second officer on a
variety of vessel types prior to joining NMM.
The fourth engineer was Polish and 29 years old. He had joined NMM 3 months before the accident
and was on his second 2-month contract on board Stena Alegra. Prior to joining NMM he had worked
as a commissioning engineer in a Polish shipyard for about 4 years. He held a Polish STCW III/1 OOW
Engineering Unlimited Certificate.
All Officers on board Stena Alegra held appropriate UK Certificates of Equivalent Competency enabling
them to serve on UK registered vessels.
Stena Alegra was conventionally manned with a master, chief, second and third officer in the deck
department, and a chief, second, third and fourth engineer officer in the engine department.
The master, chief officer, chief engineer and second engineer worked daywork and were not part of the
regular watchkeeping routine. The second officer and third engineer kept the 0000-0600 and 1200-1800
watches. The third officer and fourth engineer kept the 0600-1200 and 1800-2400 watches.
Two ABs were assigned to each bridge watch.
Safety management system
NMM’s safety management system (SMS) provided instructions and guidance on anchoring, which
included a statement recognising that Ro-Ro and RoPax vessels did not routinely anchor. It also advised
masters to carefully consider the following when anchoring: ‘depth of water; nature of the bottom; ship
type and condition; weather and tidal conditions; proximity of dangers; length of stay.’ The advice also
included a warning that, should two anchors be used in strong weather conditions, then the second one
should be recovered as soon as possible when the conditions moderate to prevent the anchor cables
fouling.
In addition to the written instructions and guidance, a checklist was provided. The checklist required an
anchor plan to be prepared, which considered: ‘speed reduction in ample time; direction/strength of wind
and current; tidal stream when manoeuvring at low speed; need for adequate sea room particularly to
seaward; depth of water; type of seabed; and the scope of the anchor cable required.’
Industry guidance on anchoring
The Nautical Institute publication entitled ‘Mooring and Anchoring Ships – Principles and Practice’
provides detailed information regarding anchoring operations and associated equipment. It references
assumed worst conditions for vessels at anchor, discusses methods of anchoring, and suggests
14 Roll on, Roll off
15 International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers 1978, as amended
6
considerations for deciding the amount of anchor cable to deploy. A commonly used formula for
calculating the minimum number of shackles of anchor cable to deploy is 1.5 x square root of the water
depth (measured in metres).
The Nautical Institute publication ‘Bridge Watchkeeping’ provides practical guidance on anchoring
operations and the keeping of an anchor watch. The guidance includes the recognised best practice of
fixing the vessel’s position at the time of letting go the anchor, allowing a measured distance from the
anchor to the bridge when the vessel is brought up, and constructing a swinging circle. This practice was
not followed on Stena Alegra.
Design limitations of anchoring equipment
The IACS16 ‘Requirements concerning mooring, anchoring and towing’ includes the following in respect
of the design of anchoring equipment:
‘The anchoring equipment required herewith is intended for temporary mooring of a vessel within a
harbour or sheltered area when the vessel is awaiting berth, tide, etc;
The equipment is therefore not designed to hold a ship off fully exposed coasts in rough weather…;
The anchoring equipment presently required herewith is designed to hold a ship in good holding
ground in conditions such as to avoid dragging of the anchor...;
The Equipment Numeral (EN) formula for anchoring equipment required here under is based on an
assumed current speed of 2.5 m/sec, wind speed of 25 m/sec and a scope of chain cable between 6
and 10, the scope being the ratio between length of chain out and water depth.’ [sic]
Similar accidents
On 26 November 2011, the port windlass of the UK registered Ro-Ro vessel Norcape suffered
catastrophic damage during an attempt to weigh anchor after experiencing a wind speed of up to 50
knots17. Rather than keep the vessel underway or seek a less exposed location, the master had opted to
anchor the vessel with 8 shackles of anchor cable deployed in a water depth of 35 metres. Even though
a second anchor had been lowered onto the seabed to reduce anticipated yaw, the vessel’s heading
was noted to swing through 150º. A safety flyer that accompanied the MAIB’s safety investigation report
strongly advised an owner or operator to ensure that its SMS provides masters with clear guidance on
the capability of its vessel’s anchoring system, including:
• Any limitations of the anchor system components, including those of the windlass.
• Effects of windage in various load conditions.
• Risks associated with excessive yaw.
On 1 January 2002, the Cyprus registered product tanker Willy grounded after dragging its anchor in a
wind speed of up to 24 knots18. The vessel had been anchored 0.4 mile off a leeshore with 4 shackles of
anchor cable deployed in a water depth of 10 metres. The MAIB safety investigation report concluded
that insufficient anchor cable had been deployed, and that the vessel’s close proximity to the shore,
together with the speed at which it dragged its anchor, provided insufficient time for the engine to be
started and for the crew to take effective corrective action.
16 International Association of Classification Societies
17 MAIB Report No 28/2012
18 MAIB Report No 31/2002
7
ANALYSIS
The master decided to anchor Stena Alegra with forecast winds of up to 47 knots. Insufficient
contingency planning meant that the possibility of winds in excess of those forecast, and measures to
reduce the consequent increased risk of the vessel dragging its anchor and grounding when anchored in
such close proximity to land, had not been considered. The vessel dragged its anchor while encountering
wind speeds that were well in excess of its anchoring equipment design parameters, and grounded due
to insufficient corrective action being taken in the limited time available.
The decision to anchor
Stena Alegra was required to layover from Monday morning until its scheduled loading time on Tuesday
afternoon. Three vessels routinely used the same Ro-Ro berth in Karlskrona. Consequently, Stena
Alegra was required to leave the berth after discharge, which left the master with a choice of either
leaving the port and proceeding to sea, or anchoring in one of the designated anchorage areas within the
port approaches until the berth became available the following day.
The weather forecast available to the master at the time of his decision to anchor was for winds to
increase up to 47 knots from the south-west. The master considered there would be little protection
from the wind and sea immediately outside the port because of the port’s southerly location. He also
assessed that the small islands surrounding the designated anchorages within the port approaches
would provide an adequate lee for Stena Alegra.
In dismissing the option of proceeding to sea, the master did not consider steaming east or west along
the coast from Karlskrona, and then heaving to in areas where the sea conditions were likely to have
been more favourable due to the shelter provided by the Swedish coast. Such an option was feasible
considering the length of the layover period (Figure 3).
The master’s decision to anchor was influenced by his previous successful, albeit limited, experience
of anchoring other Ro-Ro and RoPax vessels in wind speeds of about 40 knots. His lack of experience
of anchoring Stena Alegra was due mainly to the short time that he had been on board, and the limited
opportunities he had had to observe how the vessel performed at anchor. His lack of familiarity with
Stena Alegra’s anchoring capabilities were further exacerbated by the limited experience of both the
outgoing master and the officers and crew in general, none of whom had witnessed the vessel anchored
in strong winds.
Stena Alegra was a recent acquisition for NMM. Therefore, in familiarising themselves with its
capabilities and performance, the crew were reliant on information exchanged during handover periods,
and instructions and guidance held on board, some of which is likely to have been lost during the vessel’s
change of management.
Although the forecast wind speed was at the assumed maximum design limit of Stena Alegra’s anchoring
equipment, the yawing effect of the vessel would have increased the loading to beyond that limit. NMM’s
SMS did not refer to this information. Had such guidance been available on board, it might have deterred
the master from his decision to proceed to anchor.
Lack of crew familiarity with a vessel’s capabilities and performance, and the need for clear guidance to
be provided in a company’s SMS, featured in the MAIB’s safety investigation report and accompanying
flyer following the accident on board Norcape.
Having decided that anchoring the vessel in the forecast wind was feasible, Stena Alegra’s master
then needed to carefully appraise his intended anchorage, fully assess the consequent risks, plan the
anchoring operation and implement appropriate safeguards to prevent the vessel dragging anchor and/or
running aground.

Appraisal of anchorage
There were two designated anchorages within the approaches to Karlskrona. The master selected
anchorage B because in anchorage A Stena Alegra would have potentially impeded the passage of other
vessels using the Ro-Ro berth. He decided to anchor the vessel south-west of its normal anchoring
position so as to maximise its distance from Aspeskarsklapparna, without unduly encroaching into the
main entrance channel. He also increased the amount of anchor cable normally used, to 8 shackles
which, in a water depth of 15 metres, provided a scope of 14.7 (ie greater than the assumed maximum
scope in the IACS design requirements for anchoring equipment). The pilot’s comments regarding the
suitability of the holding ground at the master’s intended anchoring position provided tacit validation of
the appropriateness of his decision to proceed to anchor in anchorage B despite the forecast weather
conditions.
In modifying Stena Alegra’s normal anchoring position and increasing the amount of cable normally
used, the master broadly took into consideration the factors listed in the NMM’s SMS.
However, the master did not construct a swinging circle for the vessel either at the planning stage or after
anchoring. Had he done so, he might have identified the potential for Stena Alegra to pass over Lassa
Grund north cardinal mark, and the vessel’s close proximity to Aspeskarsklapparna (Figure 4). Taking
into account Stena Alegra’s windage area, this graphical illustration might have alerted the master to
the limited time that he would have available in which to arrest the vessel’s drift should it start to drag its
anchor, and might have encouraged him to reconsider his decision to anchor.
Finally, the master did not consider the possibility of the vessel experiencing stronger winds than those
forecast. A higher wind speed increased the potential for the anchoring equipment to fail or the vessel to
drag its anchor, and for an increased rate of drift reducing the time available before the vessel grounded.
With no contingency plan developed in the event of stronger winds than forecast being experienced, the
trigger point at which a response was executed became the point at which the vessel eventually started
to drag its anchor.
Monitoring of vessel at anchor
As the wind increased during the afternoon of 28 October, Stena Alegra maintained its position, which
reaffirmed to the master that the amount of cable deployed was probably sufficient to prevent the vessel
dragging its anchor in the forecast conditions. Additionally, if the vessel did start to drag its anchor,
he remained confident that, by clutching in No 3 main engine, the vessel’s drift could be satisfactorily
arrested to prevent it from grounding.
However, once the wind had increased to over 40 knots, the master became concerned by the erratic
and severe yawing of the vessel. This behaviour can be explained by the position of the vessel’s hawse
pipe which, owing to the bow door, was situated further aft on the shoulder than that on a conventional
vessel, and to the effect of the wind on the forward accommodation block. The combined effect of these
factors was a tendency for the vessel to present itself beam onto the wind, particularly during gusts.
The erratic yawing of the vessel prompted the master to consider what options might be available to him.
There is conflicting evidence suggesting that he might have been influenced by a misinterpretation of the
‘Sea State Restriction’ of 4 metres listed on the vessel’s ‘Operational Limits’ certificate in not deciding to
proceed to sea. However, once the wind had increased to 50 knots, he considered it to be too dangerous
for the vessel to safely pass through the narrow gap between Aspo and Tjurko.
Having decided to remain at anchor, the master could have taken proactive measures to reduce the risk
of the vessel dragging its anchor and grounding. No 3 main engine could have been clutched in, and all
other main engines, steering motors and thrusters could have been started and placed on bridge control.

The master could then have manoeuvred the vessel ahead to reduce the loading on the anchoring
equipment. He could also have lowered the port anchor to the seabed to reduce the vessel’s yawing.
Although NMM’s SMS referred to the possibility of using two anchors in strong weather conditions, it
made no reference to using the second anchor for this purpose. He might also have considered paying
out more anchor cable, although this would have reduced the vessel’s distance from the leeshore and so
decreased the time available in which to prevent it from grounding.
Had the master prepared a contingency plan to respond to changes in observed wind conditions rather
than to simply react to the vessel dragging its anchor, he might have included the above measures
in that plan. Such action required a greater level of proficiency and precautionary thought than that
demonstrated. Instead, the master remained hopeful that the wind would peak before the vessel started
to drag its anchor, and was confident that the main engines would be available for use in sufficient time
to prevent it from grounding.
Dragging of anchor and grounding
When Stena Alegra started to drag its anchor the wind speed had increased to 66 knots observed on
the anemometer by the master (a maximum of 76 knots was recorded on the vessel’s VDR19). Such
wind speeds were about 50% higher than those for which the vessel’s anchoring equipment had been
designed, and it is therefore unsurprising that the vessel dragged its anchor at this stage.
The early identification that Stena Alegra was dragging its anchor failed to prevent it grounding because
of the vessel’s close proximity to the leeshore, and the crew having insufficient time in which to
respond. The main engines were at 5 minutes’ notice and were made ready within this time. However,
Stena Alegra quickly reached a speed of 3 knots when dragging, and covered the short distance to
Aspeskarsklapparna in 4 minutes. Having the main engines at 5 minutes’ notice, with the trigger point for
their use being when the vessel started to drag its anchor, was inappropriate and is indicative that the
master did not appreciate the vessel’s likely rate of drift in such circumstances.
The MAIB safety investigation report of the accident involving Willy highlighted the rate at which the
vessel dragged its anchor, allowing insufficient time for the crew to prevent it from grounding.
The master expected No 3 main engine to be immediately clutched in when requested, and he had
left written instructions on the bridge to this effect. However, his verbal instructions were for the main
engines to remain on 5 minutes’ notice. The fourth engineer’s understanding was that No 3 main engine
was running, and ready to be clutched in, to reduce the time needed to have all main engines ready for
use to satisfy the master’s 5 minutes’ notice requirement.
The differing interpretations of the master’s requirement for the main engines’ readiness remained
unresolved throughout the vessel’s time at anchor. Therefore, when the third officer called the fourth
engineer to “start the second engine quickly and clutch in the first”, the instruction failed to transmit
the master’s expectation for No 3 main engine to be clutched in and its control passed to the bridge
immediately.
No 3 main engine could, in fact, have been clutched in from the bridge, a function that none of the bridge
team were aware of. However, it is uncertain whether the immediate use of a single main engine would
have prevented the vessel from grounding in the prevailing conditions.
19 Voyage Data Recorder
12
CONCLUSIONS
• The master decided to anchor Stena Alegra with wind conditions forecast to increase to the assumed
design limitation of its anchoring equipment. In doing so, he did not take into account the additional
loading that would be caused by the vessel yawing, and did not consider contingency options should
the wind speed increase to beyond that forecast.
• In dismissing an option of proceeding to sea, the master did not consider steaming a short distance
along the coast and to then heave to in areas where the sea conditions were likely to have been more
favourable. He might also have misinterpreted the ‘Sea State Restriction’ of 4 metres listed on the
vessel’s ‘Operational Limits’ certificate.
• The master’s decision to anchor was influenced by his previous successful, albeit limited, experience
of anchoring other Ro-Ro and RoPax vessels in winds of about 40 knots. He lacked familiarity with
Stena Alegra’s capabilities and performance when anchored due to his limited time on the vessel and
a lack of available guidance on board.
• The master did not construct a swinging circle for the vessel. Had he done so, he might have been
alerted to the vessel’s close proximity to danger and the limited time that he would have available to
arrest its drift should it start to drag its anchor.
• Had the master prepared a contingency plan to respond to changes in observed wind conditions rather
than waiting for the vessel to drag its anchor, he could have taken proactive measures to prevent the
grounding.
• The master lacked an appreciation of the vessel’s likely rate of drift should it start to drag anchor in
the prevailing wind conditions. His expectation for No 3 main engine to be clutched in immediately if
the vessel dragged its anchor was not effectively communicated to the engine control room. However,
if No 3 main engine had been clutched in immediately, it is uncertain that its sole use would have
prevented the vessel from grounding.
13
ACTION TAKEN
Actions taken by other organisations
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency has:
Undertaken to revise the wording of its ‘Operational Limits’ certificate pro forma to remove any potential
for confusion regarding the meaning of ‘Sea State Restrictions’.
Northern Marine Management Ltd has:
Carried out its own internal investigation into the accident, and:
• Conducted additional audits of its Ro-Ro and RoPax vessels, focusing on the standard of
management and navigation practices on board.
• Held 2-day seminars for senior officers at its head office to encourage communication and,
specifically, to discuss this accident.
• Conducted a review of its SMS anchoring and heavy weather procedures with the intention of
ensuring lessons learned from this accident are incorporated.
• Issued a fleet circular with amendments to be incorporated in the next revision of its SMS Manual.
14
RECOMMENDATIONS
Northern Marine Management Ltd is recommended to:
2014/118 Improve its safety management system by:
• Providing specific guidance on the operational limitations of vessels’ anchoring
equipment.
• Providing further guidance to masters on its expectations for anchor planning, including
the importance of contingency planning and the need for early action to prevent a
vessel dragging its anchor.
• Enhancing its masters’ handover procedures to ensure that key information regarding
a vessel’s capabilities and performance while at anchor are discussed during handover
periods.
Safety recommendations shall in no case create a presumption of blame or liability

title: Grounding of semi-submersible rig Transocean Winner after the loss of tow from tug ALP Forward
text:
Grounding of semi-submersible rig Transocean Winner after the loss of tow from tug ALP Forward
Location: Isle of Lewis, Scotland.
From:
Marine Accident Investigation Branch
Published:
7 September 2017
Vessel type:
Merchant vessel 100 gross tons or over
Report type:
Investigation report
Date of occurrence:
8 August 2016
Accident Investigation Report 19/2017
MAIB investigation report 19-2017: Transocean Winner and ALP Forward
Annexes to MAIB investigation report 19-2017: Transocean Winner and ALP Forward
MAIB drone footage
Summary
At 0652 on 8 August 2016, the Marshall Islands registered semi-submersible rig Transocean Winner grounded on the Isle of Lewis following the loss of tow from the Dutch registered tug ALP Forward. The tug and tow was on passage from Stavanger, Norway to Valletta, Malta when it encountered severe weather west of the Hebrides. The effect of the wind and waves on Transocean Winner led to the loss of ALP Forward’s ability to control the direction and speed of the tug and tow. After being dragged backwards by the tow for over 24 hours, the tow line, weakened by the repeated sudden loadings, parted and the tug was unable to pick up the emergency towline.
Safety lessons
the effect of the wind on Transocean Winner led to ALP Forward being incapable of controlling the wind and tow in the severe weather conditions. Without the necessary information, it was not possible for the master to predict the tug’s inability to hold the rig and change his passage plan in time to seek shelter
the planning of a passage so close to the coast left little sea room for the tug and tow to drift. When ALP Forward lost control of the tug and tow, it was very likely that Transocean Winner would have grounded even if the tow line had not parted
the tow line was in a generally poor condition, there was insufficient catenary in the deployed tow line which led, in the weather conditions, to repeated sudden loadings resulting in the tow line parting. It is quite possible that a new tow line would have also parted under the same circumstances and conditions
Supporting document
TTI Testing Ltd report to MAIB on the inspection and testing of failed tow wire rope from tug ALP Forward
Video extract from TTI rope tests
Recommendations
ALP Maritime Services has been recommended (2017/135) to review its procedures with regard to the production of towing manuals to ensure that the guidance provided in them:
complies with the guidelines issued by the International Maritime Organization in MSC/Circ.884 of 1998
provides those responsible for the safety of the tow with all the necessary information, including tow-specific guidance on:
the need to consider sea room and lee shores during passage planning
the provision of an adequate catenary
the need to report when control of the tow is lost
the limitations/ functionality of the emergency towing arrangement when in adverse weather
provides its vessels’ crews and maintenance staff with comprehensive guidance on the maintenance, inspection and discard of tow lines

SYNOPSIS
At 0652 on 8 August 2016, the Marshall Islands registered semi-submersible rig
Transocean Winner grounded on the north coast of the Isle of Lewis, Scotland. The
grounding followed the loss of tow from ALP Forward, a Dutch registered anchor handling
tug. The rig’s starboard pontoon was damaged during the grounding, leading to the loss of
approximately 53m3 of diesel oil. The diesel oil was broken up by the rough seas and there
was no pollution of the shoreline. Transocean Winner was refloated on 22 August.
The tug and tow was on passage from Stavanger, Norway to Valletta, Malta when it
encountered severe weather west of the Hebrides. The effect of the wind and waves on
Transocean Winner overcame ALP Forward’s ability to control the tug and tow which were
dragged backwards for over 24 hours until the tow line parted. The emergency tow line was
not accessible and Transocean Winner ran aground on the north coast of the Isle of Lewis.
Examination established that ALP Forward’s tow line was in a deteriorated condition before
the tow commenced, and it was further weakened during the heavy weather prior to the
accident.
The MAIB investigation found that, once the effect of the wind on Transocean Winner had
taken control of the tug and tow, the grounding was very likely regardless of whether the
tow line held or parted. The emergency towing vessel Herakles was situated in Kirkwall,
Orkney some 12 hours transit time from Lewis. It was unable to arrive at the accident site
before Transocean Winner grounded. However, had the emergency towing vessel been on
scene, it is very unlikely that it would have been able to provide any practical assistance in
maintaining control of Transocean Winner or preventing the grounding.
ALP Forward’s capabilities satisfied industry requirements but the master had insufficient
information to predict that the tug would be unable to hold the rig in the forecast weather.
Owners and warranty surveyors ashore were not able to provide timely assistance due to
ineffective monitoring of the daily reports, and the emergency towing arrangement was
unsuitable for use in poor weather.
Transocean Winner’s owner has started an internal investigation and taken action to ensure
that all parties, both on-site and ashore, are fully engaged with the planning and monitoring
of similar tows in the future.
ALP Maritime Services BV has been recommended to review its procedures with regard
to the production of Towing Manuals to ensure that they provide those responsible for
the safety of the tow with all the necessary information, and to provide comprehensive
guidance on the maintenance, inspection and discard of tow lines.
