In May 2022, the MAIB issued an interim report on the investigation into the fatal accident
on board Cornishman. The interim report highlighted that an arrangement containing a
chain passing over a static pin makes it very difficult to calculate the tensile strength of the
arrangement and makes it more susceptible to failure. The interim report further stated that:
It is therefore imperative in the short-term that these types of release mechanisms and
derrick head pins are subject to regular inspection and replaced at the earliest sign
of wear.
Alternative arrangements for the quick-release mechanisms at the derrick head that either do
not include a chain passing over a static pin, or remove the risk of the gear falling in the event of
a failure, have been fitted to vessels to mitigate the risk of gear falling from height in the event
of a failure of the chain arrangement. The alternative configurations observed by the MAIB have
included the use of wire and sheave arrangements (Figure 4), the replacement of the derrick
head arrangement with a swinging arm mechanism (Figure 5), and the provision of warp tension
monitoring and release systems. Options have also been suggested for a secondary means of
retaining the gear, in addition to the chain, to prevent the gear from falling in the event of a chain
failure while still allowing the release of the gear in an emergency (Figure 6).

The initial stages of the investigation have identified that:
● The recent recorded accidents and failures of chain links leading over a static pin as part of
a quick-release mechanism indicate the significant risk of such arrangements failing when
loads are applied to the chains. These arrangements can induce complex loading forces in
the chain links, leading to excessive wear on the chain links and significantly reducing the

chain links may not be easily visible mean that it can be difficult to inspect and identify
issues with the quick-release arrangement.

crew members working on the deck below.

Partial collapse of an inflatable migrant boat resulting in the loss of 1 life on 9 September 2025
Location: English Channel.
From:
Marine Accident Investigation Branch
Published:

Accident Investigation Report 21/2026
Read our marine accident investigation report, which includes what happened, subsequent actions taken and recommendations.
MAIB investigation report 21-2026: inflatable migrant boat
Summary
On 9 September 2025, an inflatable migrant boat partially collapsed during a rescue operation by a Border Force vessel in the English Channel, resulting in one fatality. As the Border Force vessel approached, a sudden shift in the occupants on board the migrant boat caused one side to collapse, resulting in significant flooding and panic. Multiple persons entered the water, and the casualty was trampled into the bottom of the boat, causing her to drown. Once the casualty had been identified, Border Force vessel’s crew were unable to recover her until specialist search and rescue assets arrived on scene.
Safety issues
The boat was a rudimentary craft produced outside recognised safety standards and was wholly unsuitable for crossing the English Channel. Its poor construction, overcrowding, low freeboard and deteriorated condition made it vulnerable to flooding and collapse.
The casualty was not identified promptly because the crew were managing a mass rescue from a rapidly deteriorating boat. Her position in the flooded boat, partial submersion and lack of conspicuity reduced the likelihood of early detection.
The crew of the attending Border Force vessel could not safely recover an unresponsive casualty from within the collapsed boat using the training, procedures and equipment available to them. Recovery therefore depended on the arrival of dedicated search and rescue assets.
Recommendations
Border Security Command is recommended to:
Review its training and operational procedures to improve the early identification of inflatable boat occupants who may be in difficulty, unresponsive, partially submerged or otherwise less visible during rescue operations. This is in order to enable a timely response to people in distress, to address the risk of delayed rescue and loss of life.
To develop, with relevant partner organisations, procedures, training and equipment to enable the safe recovery of an unresponsive casualty from a partially or fully collapsed inflatable boat. This is to include a risk-based framework as to when recovery can be attempted without exposing responders to unacceptable risk. This is in order to increase the likelihood of successful casualty rescue in scenarios where the boat is compromised, to address the risk of fatalities resulting from delays to rescue.

SYNOPSIS
On 9 September 2025, an inflatable boat carrying
74 migrants across the English Channel partially
collapsed during a rescue operation by the Border Force
vessel BF Volunteer. One of the occupants, 36-year-old
Manpreet Kaur, was found submerged in the flooded boat
and subsequently died from drowning.
United
The migrants had been provided with the boat by
Kingdom
criminal facilitators. During the crossing from France,
the overcrowded and unseaworthy boat progressively
deteriorated as it lost air, accumulated water and spilt
fuel, reducing both buoyancy and structural integrity.
At 1057, when the boat entered UK waters, it was
declared to be in distress and BF Volunteer was tasked
France
to rescue those on board. As a line was passed during
the intercept, the occupants moved rapidly to one side,
causing the port sponson to collapse. This resulted in
further flooding, multiple people entering the water and
the development of a mass casualty situation.
During the incident, Manpreet Kaur was trampled into the bottom of the boat and became
submerged in a mixture of water and fuel. She was not identified immediately and remained
submerged for a prolonged period before recovery. Although all visible survivors were
rescued quickly, her eventual recovery by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution and the
commencement of resuscitation occurred after a period of submersion beyond which
survival was highly unlikely.
The investigation found that the migrant boat was wholly unsuitable for the voyage. Its poor
construction, overcrowding, low freeboard and unsafe fuel and engine arrangement made it
vulnerable to flooding and collapse.
The investigation also found that Border Force procedures, training and equipment did not
address the recovery of an unresponsive casualty from within a partially collapsed inflatable
boat, exposing a limitation in on-scene capability when rescue conditions deteriorated.
Recommendations have been made to Border Security Command to improve the
identification of less visible or unresponsive occupants during rescue operations, and to
develop procedures, training and equipment to enable the safe recovery of an unresponsive
casualty from a partially or fully collapsed inflatable boat.

1.2 BACKGROUND
Since 2018, attempts to cross the English Channel in small boats have developed
into a persistent and complex maritime safety issue, and placed sustained demands
on UK search and rescue (SAR) and border enforcement agencies. The scale of this
activity has also significantly increased: 299 people arrived by small boat in 2018
compared to 41,472 in 2025.
The nature of crossings also evolved during this period. The average number
of people carried on each boat markedly increased, reaching 62 people per
boat in 2025, while some boats carried more than 120 people. The boats used
were typically inflatable craft manufactured on the black market, at scale.
They were operated by people with little or no maritime experience and put
to sea without effective lifesaving appliances, creating an inherently high-risk
operating environment.
The MAIB previously investigated two accidents involving migrant boats in the
English Channel: the loss of at least 27 people in November 2021, when an
inflatable boat carrying about 33 occupants flooded and partially sank; and the loss
of at least eight people in December 2022, after another overcrowded inflatable boat
suffered structural failure (see section 1.11). Both investigations identified common
safety issues, including unseaworthy and overloaded boats, limited lifesaving
equipment, and difficulties locating, monitoring and assisting multiple small craft in a
congested maritime environment.
The UK government’s operational response to small boat crossings significantly
matured since these earlier accidents. The MAIB’s investigation into the
November 2021 tragedy noted that the rapid increase in crossings had initially
outpaced elements of the UK response, particularly in relation to surveillance,
coordination and situational awareness. Subsequent capability improvements and
the development of a more coordinated interagency approach strengthened the UK’s
ability to respond.
By 2025, the operational context in which this accident occurred was materially
different from that examined in MAIB’s earlier migrant boat investigations. This report
therefore considered an accident that arose within a more established response
system, while recognising that the fundamental risks associated with small,
overloaded and unseaworthy boats remain unchanged.
1.3 NARRATIVE
1.3.1 Departure from France
In the early hours of 9 September 2025, a group of migrants were transported to
an unidentified location along the inshore canal system at Malo-les-Bains, northern
France. Each had paid criminal organisations to facilitate their passage to the UK.
On arrival, gang members provided an inflatable boat, an outboard engine, fuel and
manual pumps for the group to inflate the boat. While inflating the boat’s deck, they
found that the pump could not be removed from the valve without the deck deflating,
so it remained connected.
3
After launching into a nearby canal, the boat proceeded towards the sea, collecting
additional groups of migrants, including Manpreet Kaur, along the route and from
the beach. Those boarding from the beach waded out into chest-deep water before
being assisted on board. At several of the boarding points improvised stalls sold
lifejackets, which some of the occupants, including Manpreet, wore.
At 0344, the boat departed France (Figure 1) for the UK with 74 people on board. It
was logged within minutes by Dover Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC).
About 30 minutes later, the French SAR vessel Minck intercepted the boat and
shadowed it for the remainder of its voyage towards UK territorial waters.
Figure 1: Chart showing departure and rescue position of migrant boat 512
1.3.2 Crossing and deterioration
During the passage Manpreet Kaur was seated aft, on the deck and away from
the sponsons, in confined conditions alongside other occupants (Figure 2). As
the voyage progressed, the boat began to take on water, resulting in a significant
accumulation on the deck. Occupants attempted to bail out the water using small
containers such as plastic bottles. The sponsons progressively lost buoyancy,
and repeated reinflation of the deck was required as the pump became detached
allowing air to escape under pressure. The engine required refuelling on at least four
occasions, during which petrol was spilled into the bottom of the boat.
4
By this stage, the occupants had very little space and many were sitting on or
against one another. Those seated low in the centre of the boat were partially
submerged for much of the voyage, and the water in places was more than
knee-deep by the time of rescue. The mixture of seawater and petrol caused
chemical burns to several occupants, including Manpreet.
The boat deteriorated further as the crossing continued, resulting in reduced rigidity
and freeboard and increased water accumulation. Before entering UK territorial
waters, several physical and verbal altercations occurred on board and many of the
occupants feared for their safety.
The voyage was prolonged with confined conditions. Many of the boat's occupants
became cold, dehydrated and weak by the time of rescue; some temporarily lost full
use of their legs.

1.3.3 Rescue and collapse
At 1057, the boat, by then designated as migrant boat 512, entered the UK search
and rescue region and was formally declared to be in distress by His Majesty’s
Coastguard (HMCG) Dover MRCC. The Border Force1 Crew Transfer Vessel (CTV)
BF Volunteer, which had been tasked with rescuing the boat’s occupants, began its
approach. At that time, Manpreet remained seated towards the back of the boat and
had started to complain to fellow occupants that she felt dizzy. About 10 minutes
later, as BF Volunteer continued its approach, Manpreet was seen sitting up for the
last time.

1.3.4 Recovery of occupants and discovery of the casualty
By 1114, all those in the water had been recovered on board either BF Volunteer or
Osprey III and migrant boat 512 had been brought alongside. The boat’s remaining
occupants were then recovered onto BF Volunteer’s deck via the aft platform.
During this process, at 1119, the BF Volunteer deck team noticed that a person
was face down and partially submerged in among a large quantity of floating debris
towards the aft end of migrant boat 512. The deck team immediately reported this to
BF Volunteer’s master and officer in charge (OIC), who were in the wheelhouse.
The crew, the master and the OIC discussed the possibility of recovering Manpreet
from the bottom of migrant boat 512. They concluded that it would be too dangerous,
given that the boat was collapsed, flooded and lacked a solid deck. This information
was relayed to the UK Border Force team embedded within Dover MRCC.
By 1121, all the occupants of migrant boat 512 had been rescued except Manpreet.
With nobody left on board to hold the line the boat began to drift away, requiring
BF Volunteer to manoeuvre to bring it back alongside. Once migrant boat 512 was
alongside, further assessments were made as to whether a man overboard sling
could be used to retrieve Manpreet. It was agreed that entering the boat would place
the crew at unacceptable risk and the decision was to wait for SAR authorities to
arrive. Migrant boat 512 was then manoeuvred to BF Volunteer’s starboard side to
allow for the offloading of those on board Osprey III.
1.3.5 Recovery of the casualty
At 1137, R363 arrived on scene and was directed by Dover MRCC to start a search
pattern to determine whether any people had drifted away during the event. At
1145, Walmer ILB arrived on scene and two RNLI crew boarded migrant boat 512
to recover Manpreet. When they boarded, the RNLI crew sank to chest height
in the mixture of water and fuel and the recovery was physically demanding
(Figure 5). Five minutes later, Manpreet was recovered on board Walmer ILB and
cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was started. Walmer ILB then moved away
from BF Volunteer towards Dover.
At 1201, Manpreet was winched onto R363 where advanced life support was
administered. R363 proceeded to the landing pad at Dover MRCC, where an
ambulance was waiting. At 1253, recognition of life extinct was declared.

1.4 ENVIRONMENTAL
At the time of the accident the weather was fine and clear with good visibility, sunny
spells and an air temperature of 15°C. There was almost no wind, the sea state was
calm, and the sea temperature was 18.5°C.
1.5 THE DECEASED
Manpreet Kaur was a 36-year-old Indian national who had travelled alone
to northern France to reach the UK. Her personal circumstances were
otherwise unknown.
1.5.1 Postmortem examination
Manpreet Kaur’s cause of death was recorded as drowning. The postmortem
examination found no evidence of significant underlying natural disease or traumatic
injury that could explain death or loss of consciousness before immersion.
Manpreet’s body and clothing had a strong smell of fuel, and there were widespread
areas of skin loss. These findings were considered consistent with either prolonged
submersion in water or fuel contamination. The examination also noted that it was
difficult to determine the extent of Manpreet’s exposure to the fuel, but inhalation or
intoxication could not be ruled out.
1.5.2 Toxicology report
Toxicological analysis identified no alcohol, drugs or carbon monoxide. Additional
blood testing for hydrocarbons found the following substances:
● 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane (MTBE)
● toluene
● hexane
● hexanal
● acetone
● 2,3-octanedione.
The report identified toluene, hexane, hexanal and acetone as compounds that may
be present in postmortem samples as a result of decomposition or degradation, with
acetone also capable of arising through postmortem microbial activity. Although
MTBE and 2,3-octanedione were not identified as recognised decomposition
products, the toxicologist did not exclude decomposition as a possible source for
either compound.
9
1.5.3 Fuel additives
Toluene was used in petrol to enhance octane performance. Hexane was a naturally
occurring constituent of petrol and typically formed a small proportion of its volume,
contributing to volatility, particularly at lower temperatures. MTBE was added as
a fuel oxygenate to improve combustion efficiency and reduce emissions. MTBE
concentrations in postmortem blood and urine have been used in previous forensic
cases as indicators of petrol exposure.
Petrol fume inhalation could cause dose dependent effects on the central nervous,
cardiac and respiratory systems. Lower levels of exposure could cause irritation
and mild cognitive impairment, while higher concentrations could cause narcosis,
unconsciousness and fatal arrhythmias. Severe exposure could also displace
oxygen, causing hypoxia. In some cases, death could occur suddenly due to cardiac
sensitisation or respiratory failure.
1.6 MIGRANT BOAT 512
1.6.1 Construction
Migrant boat 512 was 7.8m long with a beam of 2.2m. Its sponsons, hull and deck
were constructed from unreinforced PVC. The sponsons were divided into four
separate chambers, each fitted with a valve with a spring-loaded pin that could be
set to inflate or deflate. The deck was a single drop-stitch chamber with its own
valve and was not secured to the rest of the boat. Several securing points had been
glued to the sponsons along the boat’s length. The transom was taped and glued in
place (Figure 6) and was constructed from non-marine grade plywood.
The boat’s origin was unknown. Such vessels were commonly produced from
low-cost materials in workshops or factories operating outside recognised safety and
quality standards.
1.6.2 Boat defects
The deck valve leaked during inflation unless the pump remained connected. The
MAIB tested the boat’s valves and found no obvious defects, although the deck
valve could not be tested under pressure because the boat was no longer airtight
at the time of inspection. Several glued-on securing points had detached from the
sponsons (Figure 6). The sponsons lost air during the voyage, with small tears
reported in the boat.
1.6.3 Engine and fuel
Migrant boat 512 was fitted with a 9.9 horsepower (hp) four-stroke outboard engine
connected to a 12-litre external fuel tank. The engine consumed about 3.5 litres of
fuel per hour. Two additional 10-litre jerrycans were also carried on board (Figure 7).
No refuelling equipment was provided, and fuel was spilled into the boat each time
the tank was replenished. The lower section of the engine shaft was in contact
with the base of the transom at a point where the PVC had been taped, resulting in
abrasion and a hole in the structure (see Figure 6). A foam insert had been taped to
the underside of the shaft in an apparent attempt to reduce this contact.

1.6.4 Loading and freeboard
Migrant boat 512 did not have an established loading capacity, although comparable

1.7 BF VOLUNTEER
1.7.1 Vessel description
BF Volunteer (Figure 9) was a twin-hulled CTV with a registered length of 20.7m
originally built to transfer personnel to, from and between offshore wind farms. The
vessel was certified to carry up to 15 persons under the Code of Practice for the
construction, machinery, equipment, stability and examination of small commercial
vessels. Seacat Services Ltd (see section 1.8.5) had completed additional
stability calculations demonstrating the vessel’s ability to carry up to 150 more
recovered people.
BF Volunteer had open deck areas forward and aft, both of which were used as
temporary shelter areas for recovered migrants. The aft end of the port hull had
been modified to include a lower secure platform to assist the transfer of migrants
directly from small boats. The main deck accommodation comprised a crew welfare
area, with the wheelhouse located above.
13

1.7.2 Crew
At the time of the accident, BF Volunteer had 13 crew on board. Seacat Services Ltd
provided the master, chief mate and five deck marshals. Border Force provided the
OIC, three Border Force officers, a Criminal and Financial Investigation officer and
a medic.
The master had overall command of the vessel and was responsible for carrying
out the rescue operation. The master had been in the role since the start of the
CTV charter for migrant operations in the English Channel and was confident in
carrying out small boat rescue operations, including those requiring recovery from
the water. The chief mate assisted the master with navigation and other routine
wheelhouse tasks.
The OIC was a Border Force maritime commander whose role was to assist and
provide guidance to the master on migrant operations, communicate information
to colleagues in the Joint Control Room (JCR) and to manage other Border Force
personnel on board.
The remaining crew worked together on deck to carry out rescue operations. The
deck marshals physically assisted boat occupants during recovery, passed lines
and deployed safety equipment as required. The Border Force officers assisted the
deck marshals but were also responsible for the physical security and processing of
migrants once they were on board. The medic provided assistance where medical
assessment or intervention was required and the photographer documented the
scene in detail.
14
1.7.3 Equipment
In addition to the required safety equipment for a vessel of its size and type
BF Volunteer carried equipment to support rescues and mass casualty events
involving people in the water. This included deployable scramble nets, which could
be used to assist people from the water or lowered into a small boat alongside
to help occupants climb out. The vessel also carried several types of deployable
flotation aids, including horseshoes and large life rings that inflated automatically on
contact with the water.
The deck marshals wore drysuits and safety harnesses when working on the aft
platform. Crew working on deck wore an inflatable personal flotation device (PFD),
which inflated automatically on contact with water.
The vessel was also equipped with a man overboard sling fitted to a long pole.
This device was designed to facilitate the recovery of a person in the water using
the vessel’s recovery davit. The device required clear water around a casualty to
function as designed.
1.7.4 Training and familiarisation
All crew on board BF Volunteer had completed STCW2 basic safety training,
including fire prevention and firefighting, personal survival techniques and
elementary first aid. Seacat Services Ltd and Border Force personnel had also
completed additional internal training relevant to their roles. The additional internal
training did not include specialist SAR training.
All new crew members joining BF Volunteer were required to complete a
familiarisation process, facilitated by the OIC, to understand English Channel
migrant operations and what was expected of them.
1.8 ENGLISH CHANNEL SMALL BOAT RESPONSE SYSTEM
1.8.1 English Channel monitoring
Migrant boats were monitored from the point of departure using a combination
of aircraft, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and maritime assets. UK authorities
worked in coordination with the French Coastguard to maintain continuous tracking
as boats approached UK waters. Monitoring systems included live video feeds,
enabling personnel in the Border Force JCR and Dover MRCC to observe boats in
real time. Migrant boat 512 was monitored from within minutes of its departure from
France until its intercept later that morning as it passed into UK territorial waters.
1.8.2 UK Border Force
Border Force had a central operational role in responding to and monitoring
small boat migrant crossings in the English Channel, primarily through maritime
deployments under Operation Kirstead. Its five chartered CTVs and three support
RHIBs patrolled designated areas and were available for tasking by HMCG to
rescue and recover occupants from migrant boats in distress. The vessels also
supported the disruption of illegal entry into the UK. Law enforcement was the
primary statutory function of Border Force.

The JCR coordinated Border Force English Channel operations by integrating
intelligence, surveillance and asset tasking. Besides the core JCR staff,
Border Force Maritime and Aviation Support Officers (MASOs) embedded within
Dover MRCC provided an operational link with HMCG by assisting with asset
coordination, tasking support, information integration and operational liaison.
1.8.3 His Majesty’s Coastguard
His Majesty’s Coastguard was the statutory SAR authority and retained overall
responsibility for maritime distress responses, including small boat incidents. For
English Channel migrant operations, MRCC Dover acted as the operational focal
point, from where HMCG developed SAR plans, tasked assets and managed
incidents through a designated SAR mission coordinator.
To deliver SAR, HMCG tasked a mix of assets, including Border Force CTVs and
support RHIBs, RNLI lifeboats, and its own aviation and surveillance capabilities
such as helicopters, fixed-wing aircraft and UAVs, alongside other available maritime
resources in the area.
1.8.4 Royal National Lifeboat Institution
RNLI lifeboats were declared SAR assets, crewed by volunteers and were routinely
tasked by HMCG through MRCC Dover, particularly when rescue conditions
deteriorated or involved multiple persons in the water.
The RNLI assets regularly tasked to migrant incidents in the Dover Strait area
included all-weather lifeboats and ILBs from the Dover and Walmer lifeboat stations.
1.8.5 UK Border Force chartered crew transfer vessels
Seacat Services Ltd managed three of the five CTVs chartered by Border Force
to support the small boat response in the English Channel. The company was
responsible for the safe operation, commercial crewing, maintenance, regulatory
compliance and welfare of its vessels and crew. The vessels operated under
Seacats Services Ltd’s safety management system and the master’s overriding
authority at all times.
1.8.6 The system in operation
Small migrant boats that entered UK territorial waters were designated by HMCG as
being in distress unless there was credible evidence to indicate otherwise. Distress
was the highest category under SAR protocols and reflected the boats’ risk profile
due to their unseaworthiness.
Because migrant boats were tracked from departure, HMCG normally tasked an
available Border Force CTV before the boats reached UK territorial waters. In
practice, this meant that migrant boats were usually intercepted and their occupants
rescued shortly after crossing from French into UK waters.
Although migrant boats were designated as being in distress, a declared SAR
asset was not normally tasked unless the situation deteriorated to the point where
specialist capability was required. Most rescues were therefore conducted by
16
Border Force CTVs, which were not declared SAR assets. In the 2 years before the
accident, HMCG tasked declared SAR assets such as RNLI lifeboats to between 5%
and 7% of migrant boat rescues.
When a Border Force CTV intercepted a migrant boat its crew followed a prescribed
SOP to carry out a rescue operation. The CTV approached the migrant boat and
remained at a short distance to minimise wash and the risk of contact. At this
stage, the OIC and master assessed whether to declare a “Mayday”3 and request
additional SAR assistance, or to continue with the rescue. Their assessment
considered the vulnerability of those on board, the condition and suitability of the
migrant boat, environmental risks, the weather on scene, tasking from HMCG and
the CTV’s safe operating limits.
If direct rescue was considered appropriate, the crew established verbal
communication and instructed the occupants to stop the engine. Once it was safe to
do so, the CTV manoeuvred alongside and passed lines to gain control of the boat.
Dynamic risk assessments informed each stage of the operation. The occupants
were transferred in a controlled manner where conditions allowed. Lifesaving
equipment was otherwise deployed. Where available, a Border Force support RHIB
would be on scene and stand off at a distance to assist with handling the migrant
boat or recovering people from the water if required.
Early deployment of lifesaving equipment risked encouraging occupants to enter the
water, creating, or worsening, a mass casualty situation. The preferred approach
was to keep the occupants calm and recover them in a controlled manner via the
aft platform.
1.8.7 Procedures and their management
His Majesty’s Coastguard held overarching responsibility for SAR procedures and
incident management. Seacat Services Ltd was responsible for administering
the day-to-day safety and operating procedures on board its CTVs, including
BF Volunteer, while Border Force provided and administered the SOPs and risk
assessments for migrant operations.
Border Force SOPs covered the working arrangements between Border Force, CTV
operators and crews, operational capabilities, initial detection, escalation for further
assistance, roles and responsibilities, cold exposure and the response to mass
casualty events.
The Border Force ‘CTV Securing Migrant Vessels’ risk assessment set out the task
elements, control measures and risk ratings for intercepting and bringing a migrant
boat alongside a CTV. It identified the hazards of a migrant boat sinking or capsizing
alongside, with the associated risk of drowning, and the risk of injury while passing a
line with a chock attached. The ‘Multi-Casualty Incident’ risk assessment addressed
the hazards associated with migrants entering the water after a boat became
compromised and detailed the control measures for recovering them.
Neither risk assessment, nor any associated procedure, identified the hazard of
people becoming trapped or stranded inside a compromised boat, or the risk of
drowning inside the boat.

1.9 REGULATION
The UK’s SAR obligations applied to the response to small migrant boats in UK
territorial waters and within the UK Search and Rescue Region. These obligations
derived from international law, including the United Nations Convention on the
Law of the Sea, 1982, Article 98, the International Convention for the Safety of
Life at Sea, 1974, as amended, and the International Convention on Maritime
Search and Rescue, 1979. Together, these instruments required the UK to maintain
arrangements for an adequate and effective SAR service.
1.10 REFERENCE INFORMATION
Research by Quan et al. (2016)4 examined observable factors at the scene of a
drowning to determine their ability to predict survival and neurological outcome.
Drawing on 24 cohort studies, the study identified submersion duration as the
most significant predictor and strongly associated longer durations with poorer
outcomes resulting in death or survival with severe neurological impairment. Shorter
submersion durations were associated with more favourable outcomes including
those who survived with good neurological function.
The study indicated that submersion durations exceeding 25 minutes were
associated with very poor outcomes. Several datasets reported 100% mortality,
while others reported poor outcomes in 96% to 99% of cases. Favourable outcomes
were described as absent or rare, with such durations considered invariably fatal.
The study identified a sigmoid relationship5 between submersion duration and
outcome, with poor outcomes rapidly increasing between durations of 10 minutes
and 25 minutes.
The study concluded that:
This information may be useful to rescuers, responding systems and agencies
in the setting where decisions to rescue and care for a drowning victim pose risk
of death to the rescuer and very high costs to the responding system. They may
contribute to the decision when to attempt a rescue versus a body retrieval.
1.11 PREVIOUS ACCIDENTS AND INCIDENTS
1.11.1 Inflatable migrant boat – partial sinking with loss of at least 27 lives
During the early hours of 24 November 2021, an overcrowded inflatable boat
carrying about 33 migrants from France flooded and partially sank while crossing
the Dover Strait, resulting in at least 27 fatalities (MAIB report 7/20236). The MAIB
investigation found that the boat was wholly unsuitable for the voyage because
it was inadequately constructed, heavily overloaded and lacked basic lifesaving
equipment. The occupants had no effective means of raising an accurate distress
alert other than mobile phones, which limited the ability of rescue services to locate
the boat. The investigation also identified shortfalls in the monitoring of small boats
in the English Channel and in liaison between UK and French authorities.

1.11.2 Inflatable migrant boat – partial sinking with loss of at least 8 lives
At 0300 on 14 December 2022, an inflatable migrant boat travelling from France
to the UK suffered structural failure in the Dover Strait, causing several occupants
to enter the water and resulting in at least eight fatalities (MAIB report 9/20248).
The MAIB investigation found that the boat was inherently unseaworthy because it
was poorly constructed, overcrowded and unsuitable for open sea conditions. The
occupants had no reliable means of raising a distress alert beyond mobile phones
and informal communication. SAR assets and a fishing vessel were involved in
the rescue.
1.11.3 UK Border Force incident reports
Border Force maintained records of incidents and near misses associated with
migrant boat operations in the English Channel. These reports identified recurring
safety themes, including poor boat construction, structural failure, overcrowding,
low freeboard and difficulty maintaining control during transfers. Several incidents
involved sudden or uncontrolled entry into the water, while others involved slips,
loss of balance, unpredictable occupant behaviour and injuries from exposure to
fuel contamination.
Before this accident, Border Force records contained no examples of an
unconscious casualty requiring recovery from a collapsed or partially collapsed
migrant boat. The day after this accident, an unconscious casualty was identified
early during the intercept of a heavily overloaded but intact inflatable boat. The early
identification allowed the CTV crew to rescue the casualty by rapidly unloading the
boat, then reaching over the aft platform and lifting the casualty out before providing
immediate first aid. The incident report noted the difficulty of the rescue, including
the manual handling challenges involved. The rescued person survived.

SECTION 2 – ANALYSIS
2.1 AIM
The purpose of the analysis is to determine the contributory causes and
circumstances of the accident as a basis for making recommendations to prevent
similar accidents occurring in the future.
2.2 OVERVIEW
Manpreet Kaur drowned after being trampled in the bottom of an inflatable migrant
boat while attempting to cross the English Channel. This analysis examines
the physical mechanism of her death, the condition and structural failure of
migrant boat 512, the constraints on recovery once she was identified, and the role
of the criminal operation in creating the unsafe conditions on board.
Search and rescue tasking, situational awareness and communications were not
analysed further as causal factors. However, aspects of the response system are
considered where they are necessary to explain on-scene capability, the timing of
recovery, and the delay before dedicated SAR assets could intervene.
2.3 THE ACCIDENT
2.3.1 Cause of death and petrol exposure
The postmortem examination established that the cause of Manpreet’s death
was drowning and that she had no significant underlying disease or injuries. The
toxicology report found no indication that she was under the influence of alcohol or
drugs, but further blood tests identified hydrocarbons that could be associated with
petrol exposure.
The boat’s engine was refuelled at least four times during the voyage. The
occupants were neither equipped nor trained to carry out refuelling safely and, as a
result, fuel handling was poor and petrol was spilled into the bottom of the boat. The
presence of petrol increased the risk to occupants through exposure to vapours and
contact with fuel mixed with seawater, creating a corrosive mixture that caused skin
burns to Manpreet and several other occupants. For those sitting low down in the
centre of the boat, like Manpreet, vapour concentrations were likely to be particularly
high due to the lack of air circulation caused by their proximity to the deck, the
overcrowded conditions, and low wind speeds. This effect was likely to have been
exacerbated when the boat stopped before being intercepted by BF Volunteer.
Manpreet had reported feeling dizzy shortly before the boat collapsed. This was
consistent with the possible effects of exposure to petrol vapour, which was likely to
have contributed to her reduced physical condition before she became submerged.
However, the investigation could not determine the extent or full physiological effect
of that exposure. It was therefore not possible to conclude that petrol exposure
caused Manpreet to lose consciousness or materially contributed to her death, for
which drowning remained the recorded cause.
Manpreet Kaur drowned after becoming submerged in the bottom of
migrant boat 512. Petrol fume exposure was likely to have worsened her physical
condition and reduced her ability to respond once she became submerged.
20
2.3.2 Condition of migrant boat 512
Migrant boat 512 was in a severely degraded state by the time it entered UK waters.
The inflatable sponsons were partially deflated, the deck had lost rigidity, and a
significant volume of water had accumulated on board. Air leakage from both the
sponsons and the inflatable deck required repeated attempts at reinflation during
the voyage, and the boat was likely to have departed France underinflated. Migrant
boat 512 was not constructed to any recognised design or safety standard: its
inflatable floor was not structurally connected to the boat, deck pressure could
not be maintained once the pump was removed, its seams and transom had been
taped and glued rather than welded, and no strong points were fitted for securing or
recovering it. The shaft length of the 9.9 hp outboard engine was incompatible with
the depth of the transom, causing continuous contact with the hull and progressive
deterioration of the PVC structure, allowing water to enter the boat.
The boat’s condition deteriorated as several adverse factors acted together.
Overcrowding reduced the boat’s freeboard and increased the likelihood of water
ingress during the voyage, while persistent air and water leaks undermined
buoyancy and deck rigidity. Repeated attempts to reinflate the deck had limited
effect because the supplied pump could not be used effectively without a solid
surface to push against. Combined with the number of people carried, these
deficiencies left the boat with very limited structural resilience and made it
highly vulnerable to loss of buoyancy, flooding, deformation and collapse during
the crossing.
Migrant boat 512 was a rudimentary craft produced from low-cost materials outside
recognised safety and quality standards. Its poor construction, overcrowding,
low freeboard, air leakage, water ingress and incompatible outboard engine
arrangement meant that it was wholly unsuitable for crossing the English Channel.
By the time the boat entered UK waters it was in a compromised condition and
vulnerable to structural collapse.
2.3.3 The criminal element
The circumstances leading to Manpreet’s death arose mainly from the criminal
facilitation of the voyage in a substandard and unsafe boat rather than from
deficiencies in any regulated maritime activity. Consequently, the most significant
safety issues identified by this investigation do not readily lend themselves to
conventional safety recommendations as those responsible operate outside
established regulatory and safety frameworks.
2.3.4 Initial approach, crowd response and collapse of migrant boat 512
During BF Volunteer’s initial approach, a line was passed to migrant boat 512 to
bring it alongside. The occupants then moved rapidly towards the port side, which
imposed a substantial asymmetric load on a boat that was already structurally
weakened and underinflated. The remaining freeboard, buoyancy and rigidity were
insufficient to withstand the sudden shift in weight and significant quantities of water
entered the boat. The boat partially folded and many occupants entered the water.
The initial movement to port was likely to have been a natural response to the
line being passed across, but panic escalated once the boat began to collapse.
Occupants were already subject to significant physical stressors, including
21
overcrowding, exposure to hazardous substances and fatigue, which likely reduced
their ability to respond in a controlled manner. The approach of BF Volunteer was
also likely to have created an expectation of imminent recovery and increased the
urgency among those on board to secure rescue.
The immediate cause of migrant boat 512’s collapse was the rapid collective
movement of occupants on a boat that had already lost the buoyancy and rigidity
needed to remain stable. This movement, and the boat’s already degraded
condition, created the mass casualty circumstances that left Manpreet vulnerable to
immersion and crushing within the boat.
2.3.5 Submersion and inability to self-rescue
Manpreet was trampled and forced into the bottom of the boat as the occupants
moved around following its collapse, ending up face down in a mixture of water and
fuel. A fellow occupant attempted to pull her up by her lifejacket. At about the same
time, the partially deflated deck shifted and flipped, Manpreet’s lifejacket slipped off,
and she fell face down back onto the boat’s flooded and unsupported floor.
Once Manpreet had been forced into the bottom of the boat, the conditions on
board significantly reduced the likelihood of effective self-rescue. As discussed in
section 2.3.1, it is likely that petrol exposure contributed to Manpreet feeling dizzy
before the collapse and reduced her ability to respond once she was pushed face
down into the flooded boat. However, this was one of several factors affecting
her ability to self-rescue and could not be isolated from the effects of physical
exhaustion, the absence of a stable deck, partial submersion, loss of buoyancy and
the physical obstruction caused by other occupants and debris.
Manpreet’s physical condition, the lack of a stable deck, and the conditions on board
migrant boat 512 greatly reduced her ability to self-rescue.
2.3.6 Discovery of the casualty
Manpreet was identified 11 minutes after the first line had been passed to
migrant boat 512 and about 8 minutes after she first became submerged. She was
found lying face down in the bottom of the boat, partially submerged, while several
other occupants remained on board and required rescue.
The delay in recognising Manpreet as a casualty was likely shaped by the immediate
demands of rescuing multiple visible survivors from a rapidly deteriorating boat.
Attention on board the CTV was directed towards those in the water and to the
remaining occupants still requiring rescue. Manpreet’s position in the bottom of the
boat, together with her lack of brightly coloured lifejacket and partial submersion,
made her difficult to distinguish from the surrounding debris. No occupants drew
the crew’s attention to her position as they were rescued. Combined, these factors
reduced the likelihood of Manpreet being identified promptly in a fast-moving mass
rescue operation.
Manpreet was not identified promptly because the crew were managing a mass
rescue from a rapidly deteriorating boat. Visible survivors were prioritised,
and her position, conspicuity and partial submersion reduced the likelihood of
early detection.
22
2.4 RECOVERY AND RESCUE CONSTRAINTS ON BOARD
BF VOLUNTEER
2.4.1 Physical, environmental, equipment and training constraints
The crew of BF Volunteer carried out a dynamic risk assessment to determine
whether Manpreet’s recovery from within the semi-collapsed vessel was feasible.
Neither the vessel’s crew nor the Border Force personnel had completed specialist
SAR training. Although BF Volunteer carried recovery equipment, including an aft
loading platform, inflatable flotation aids, scramble nets and a man overboard sling,
none was suitable for recovering an unconscious casualty from inside a collapsed
boat without intervention from within the boat.
The deck marshals wore drysuits but their self-inflating PFDs would have inflated
if they had entered the flooded boat, restricting movement and further increasing
the risk to them. This assessment was consistent with the subsequent recovery by
Walmer ILB, during which two RNLI crew immediately sank to chest height in the
mixture of water and fuel on entering migrant boat 512 and took just under 5 minutes
to recover Manpreet from the boat.
Entry into the boat would have exposed BF Volunteer’s crew to a high risk of
immersion and entrapment and increased the likelihood that they would also
require rescue. This risk was heightened by their lack of specialist training and the
equipment available on board.
BF Volunteer’s crew could not safely recover Manpreet from within the collapsed
boat. Intervention therefore depended on the arrival of dedicated SAR assets.
2.4.2 Evolution of the English Channel response system
Previous MAIB investigations into migrant boat accidents identified limitations
in the monitoring, coordination and situational awareness of small boats in the
English Channel. In this case, migrant boat 512 was monitored from departure
and intercepted shortly after entering UK territorial waters within a coordinated
multiagency framework. Small migrant boats entering UK waters were routinely
treated as being in distress and a Border Force CTV was typically tasked to
rescue those on board, with specialist SAR assets usually only tasked when
conditions deteriorated.
These arrangements indicated that the operational response system had developed
since the November 2021 and December 2022 migrant boat accidents described
in section 1.11, and was better able to detect, track and respond to migrant boats at
an early stage. Unlike the earlier accidents, migrant boat 512 had been monitored
from departure in coordination with French authorities and using aerial assets. Once
the boat collapsed, the operational challenge shifted from locating, monitoring and
rescuing its occupants, to managing a rapidly developing mass casualty situation at
close quarters.
The English Channel response system had developed since earlier MAIB migrant
boat investigations, improving monitoring, coordination and early rescue. However,
this accident showed that the remaining vulnerability lay in the capability available on
scene when rescue conditions deteriorated.
23
2.4.3 UK Border Force search and rescue capability
Although Border Force CTVs were routinely used to initiate and support SAR
activity, they were not declared SAR assets and Border Force was not a SAR
organisation. The procedures and risk assessments available did not specifically
address the recovery of a casualty from within a collapsed inflatable boat, and
previous incidents had not involved this scenario.
The initial response to migrant boat 512 relied on assets that were not equipped,
trained or procedurally prepared to recover an unconscious casualty from within
a compromised boat. When migrant boat 512 collapsed, there were no suitably
equipped or trained assets available on scene to carry out the required rescue
safely. This exposed a limitation in the on-scene capability when a rescue escalated
beyond the conditions normally managed by the attending CTV. Once the situation
required more advanced rescue from within a collapsed boat, intervention depended
on the arrival of dedicated and declared SAR assets such as the RNLI ILB.
The initial response relied on Border Force vessels that were not designated,
equipped or trained as SAR assets, and existing procedures did not account for
recovery from a collapsed boat. This exposed a limitation in on-scene capability
when the situation escalated beyond the conditions normally managed by the
attending CTV.
2.5 SURVIVABILITY AND TIME CRITICALITY
2.5.1 Submersion duration
Studies indicated that good outcomes following submersion were most likely
when rescue and life support were provided within 10 minutes, with the likelihood
decreasing as submersion time increased. After 10 minutes, the probability
reduced rapidly, and there were almost no reported good outcomes after more
than 25 minutes of submersion. Manpreet had been submerged for approximately
8 minutes when she was found face down in migrant boat 512. This had increased
to 26 minutes by the time R363 arrived on scene, and to 35 minutes when the
ILB arrived. It then took over 4 minutes to recover Manpreet, with CPR started
39 minutes after submersion.
Although Manpreet was found within the period associated with the highest
likelihood of survival, effective rescue and life support were not available before that
window had passed. Her submersion time exceeded 25 minutes before SAR assets
arrived on scene, a duration after which favourable outcomes were reported to be
rare or absent. Consequently, by the time CPR was started, the probability of a
successful outcome was extremely low.
Search and rescue assets had already been tasked and were on route. By the
time Manpreet was recovered she had been submerged for a duration that made
successful rescue highly unlikely.
24
2.5.2 Opportunity for earlier recovery
Manpreet had already been submerged for 8 minutes when the crew of
BF Volunteer located her. A further 3 minutes elapsed before the boat was cleared
of occupants, after which recovery onto the CTV’s deck would have required
additional time.
Regardless of the crew’s training or equipment, the practical constraints of the
situation meant that recovery could not have been immediate. The boat first had
to be cleared of occupants before Manpreet could be reached and recovered. It is
therefore highly unlikely that she could have been recovered before her submersion
time had exceeded the period associated with the highest likelihood of survival.
Consequently, while the limitations in on-scene rescue capability were significant
they might not have altered the outcome.
Even if earlier intervention was possible by the crew of BF Volunteer, the constraints
present at the point of discovery limited the opportunity to recover Manpreet before
her submersion time exceeded likely survivable limits.
25
SECTION 3 – CONCLUSIONS
3.1 SAFETY ISSUES DIRECTLY CONTRIBUTING TO THE
ACCIDENT THAT HAVE BEEN ADDRESSED OR RESULTED IN
RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Manpreet Kaur drowned after becoming submerged in the bottom of
migrant boat 512. Petrol fume exposure was likely to have worsened her physical
condition and reduced her ability to respond once she became submerged. [2.3.1]
2. Manpreet was not identified promptly because the crew were managing a mass
rescue from a rapidly deteriorating boat. Visible survivors were prioritised, and
her position, conspicuity and partial submersion reduced the likelihood of early
detection. [2.3.6]
3. BF Volunteer’s crew could not safely recover Manpreet from within the collapsed
boat. Intervention therefore depended on the arrival of dedicated SAR assets. [2.4.1]
4. The initial response relied on Border Force vessels that were not designated,
equipped or trained as SAR assets, and existing procedures did not account for
recovery from a collapsed boat. This exposed a limitation in on-scene capability
when the situation escalated beyond the conditions normally managed by the
attending CTV. [2.4.3]
5. Search and rescue assets had already been tasked and were on route. By the
time Manpreet was recovered she had been submerged for a duration that made
successful rescue highly unlikely. [2.5.1]
3.2 OTHER SAFETY ISSUES DIRECTLY CONTRIBUTING TO
THE ACCIDENT
1. Migrant boat 512 was a rudimentary craft produced from low-cost materials outside
recognised safety and quality standards. Its poor construction, overcrowding,
low freeboard, air leakage, water ingress and incompatible outboard engine
arrangement meant that it was wholly unsuitable for crossing the English Channel.
[2.3.2]
2. The circumstances that led to Manpreet’s death arose principally from the criminal
facilitation of the voyage in a substandard and unsafe boat rather than from
deficiencies in any regulated maritime activity. Consequently, the most significant
safety issues identified by this investigation do not readily lend themselves to
conventional safety recommendations as those responsible operate outside
established regulatory and safety frameworks. [2.3.3]
3. The immediate cause of migrant boat 512’s collapse was the rapid collective
movement of occupants on a boat that had already lost the buoyancy and rigidity
needed to remain stable. This movement, and the boat’s already degraded
condition, created the mass casualty circumstances that left Manpreet vulnerable to
immersion and crushing within the boat. [2.3.4]
26
4. Manpreet’s physical condition, the lack of a stable deck, and the conditions on board
migrant boat 512 greatly reduced her ability to self-rescue. [2.3.5]
5. The English Channel response system had developed since earlier MAIB migrant
boat investigations, improving monitoring, coordination and early rescue. However,
this accident showed that the remaining vulnerability lay in the capability available on
scene when rescue conditions deteriorated. [2.4.2]
6. Even if earlier intervention was possible by the crew of BF Volunteer, the constraints
present at the point of discovery limited the opportunity to recover Manpreet before
her submersion time exceeded likely survivable limits. [2.5.2]
27
SECTION 4 – ACTION TAKEN
4.1 ACTIONS TAKEN BY OTHER ORGANISATIONS
Seacat Services Ltd has updated its procedures and provided lanyards for safety
harnesses to facilitate the entry into inflatable migrant boats to assist people in
distress when appropriate and necessary.
Border Security Command has increased the crewing levels to three people on its
chartered RHIB support vessels and undertaken to increase the availability of RHIB
support during migrant boat rescues.
28
SECTION 5 – RECOMMENDATIONS
Border Security Command is recommended to:
2026/160 Review its training and operational procedures to improve the early
identification of inflatable boat occupants who may be in difficulty,
unresponsive, partially submerged or otherwise less visible during rescue
operations. This is in order to enable a timely response to people in distress,
to address the risk of delayed rescue and loss of life.
2026/161 To develop, with relevant partner organisations, procedures, training and
equipment to enable the safe recovery of an unresponsive casualty from
a partially or fully collapsed inflatable boat. This is to include a risk-based
framework as to when recovery can be attempted without exposing
responders to unacceptable risk. This is in order to increase the likelihood of
successful casualty rescue in scenarios where the boat is compromised, to
address the risk of fatalities resulting from delays to rescue.
Safety recommendations shall in no case create a presumption of blame or liability
29

Accident Investigation Report 19/2016
Investigation report into marine accident including what happened and safety lessons learned:
MAIB investigation report 19-2016: Svitzer Moira
Summary
A crew member fell and was fatally crushed as the tug Svitzer Moira was being manoeuvred alongside an unmanned tug at Royal Portbury Dock, Bristol on 29 December 2015.
Safety lessons
no tool-box talk took place, the job was deemed as routine by the crew and assumptions were made. A tool-box talk, prior to any hazardous task, is a good opportunity for all crew to have an input, and to ensure all share the same common goal
the engineer was not wearing the appropriate personal protective equipment (
PPE
) at the time of this tragic accident, though it is unlikely that its use would have changed the outcome
the investigation found shortcomings in the oversight and control of deck operations and lapses in the use of
PPE
indicative of a significant divergence between company instructions and working practices on board that had not been corrected by shore management
Recommendations
In view of the actions taken by Svitzer Marine Limited and the Bristol Port Company, no recommendations have been made in this report

The investigation found shortcomings in the oversight and control of deck operations and lapses in the
use of personal protective equipment indicative of a significant divergence between company instructions
and working practices on board that had not been corrected by shore management.
Following an internal investigation of the accident, Svitzer Marine Limited has identified a number of
remedial measures which include a review of relevant safe systems of work and their associated risk
assessments, and actions aimed at improving the safety culture on board its vessels.
In view of the actions taken following the accident, no recommendations have been made in this report.
FACTUAL INFORMATION
Narrative
At 0930 (UTC1) on 29 December 2015, Svitzer Moira’s master was requested by the Svitzer duty tug
controller to be on board Svitzer Moira at 1930 ready to assist a car carrier that was scheduled to depart
from Royal Portbury Dock at 2000. A second Svitzer tug, Porthgarth, was also scheduled to assist.
During the afternoon, both tug masters were advised that their orders had changed. They were now to
be on board for 1900 as the car carrier was no longer sailing, but shifting to another berth within the port
that was occupied by four Svitzer tugs. The intention was to use Svitzer Moira and Porthgarth to move
two other tugs, Svitzer Ellerby and Thorngarth, to a vacant berth, prior to assisting the car carrier.
The master boarded Svitzer Moira at 1900 and joined the engineer and the deckhand who were in the
mess room. The engines were running, and the tug’s mooring lines had been singled up in preparation
for moving.
Porthgarth’s crew were also on board, socialising with the engineer and deckhand, but shortly after the
master’s arrival they returned to their vessel. Svitzer Moira’s master went to the wheelhouse, leaving the
deckhand and the engineer in the mess room. He checked and accepted the handover notes that had
been left on the computer by the previous crew, and completed a departure checklist. It was dark and
there was a south-westerly breeze.
The master requested bridge control of the engines by calling the engineer on his portable radio. The
engineer acknowledged the request and proceeded from the mess room to the control room where he
transferred control of the engines to the wheelhouse. Meanwhile, the deckhand raised the gangway.
At 1918, the master requested permission from Vessel Traffic Services (VTS) for Svitzer Moira to leave
the berth. Permission was granted and, at 1920, the mooring ropes were let go.
Svitzer Moira departed its berth and was manoeuvred approximately 40 metres ahead until it was abeam
of Svitzer Ellerby, a sister vessel that was moored alongside the same quay (Figure 2). Svitzer Ellerby
was unmanned and unlit.
As Svitzer Moira came alongside Svitzer Ellerby, the deckhand, who was positioned forward, lassoed a
bitt on Svitzer Ellerby with the eye of a mooring rope. Using his portable radio, he requested some minor
adjustments to the vessel’s relative fore and aft position to Svitzer Ellerby. He then made the rope fast
and began running a second rope.

The master then applied athwartships thrust to push Svitzer Moira bodily against Svitzer Ellerby and
maintain its parallel position alongside. He looked aft and noticed that the stern rope that had been
prepared on the aft deck was unexpectedly still lying slack.
The master left the wheelhouse to get a better view of the aft deck. He could not see the engineer so
went down to the aft deck and called to the deckhand, who was now making his way aft having made the
second forward rope fast. The deckhand did not know the whereabouts of the engineer, who normally
secured the amidships rope and the stern rope. The deckhand noticed that neither rope had been made
fast and that the eye of the amidships rope was lying slack over Svitzer Ellerby’s bulwark (Figure 3). The
deckhand straddled the bulwark with the intention of boarding Svitzer Ellerby to make the amidships rope
fast. He then saw the engineer lying on and partly trapped between the longitudinal fendering of the two
tugs, in a position forward of Svitzer Moira’s bulwark gate, which was open.
3
Figure 3: Amidships mooring rope as found following accident (reconstruction)
4
He informed the master, who returned to the wheelhouse and, at 1925, called Porthgarth on VHF2 radio
to request assistance. He also advised VTS and requested medical assistance. The master then left the
wheelhouse and returned to the main deck to assist the deckhand, who was holding onto the engineer.
Porthgarth’s crew arrived quickly and also assisted the deckhand. The master then returned to the
wheelhouse to declutch the engines, which allowed Svitzer Moira to move away from Svitzer Ellerby and
so enable the engineer to be freed. The engineer was recovered onto the deck of Svitzer Ellerby and the
crew started to administer first-aid.
At 1940, an ambulance arrived on scene followed, at 1953, by two more.
At 2017, despite the efforts to save him, the engineer was declared deceased by a doctor at the scene.
Vessel
Svitzer Moira was an Azimuth Stern Drive tug, built in Japan in 1998. The tug, which had a forward
towing winch and a bollard pull of 50 tonnes, had been based at Bristol since 2012.
The wheelhouse was accessed via a stairwell from the main deck. Access to the accommodation, mess
room and engine room was also from the main deck.
On the starboard side of the main deck was a permanently attached gangway with a pivot that enabled it
to be raised or lowered as required. A bulwark gate was located aft of the gangway (Figure 4).
